session_name: Fireside Chat: Dr. Laura Taylor-Kale & Dr. Monica Gorman
title: Fireside Chat: Dr. Laura Taylor-Kale & Dr. Monica Gorman
abstract: In this fireside chat, two leading voices on industrial policy and economic security will explore the challenges and opportunities facing America's industrial base in an era of intensifying geopolitical competition. Dr. Monica Gorman, Managing Director at Crowell Global Advisors, brings over two decades of experience spanning both the public and private sectors — most recently serving as Special Assistant to the President for Manufacturing and Industrial Policy at the White House National Economic Council, where she spearheaded the establishment of the White House Council on Supply Chain Resilience and led the nation's Supply Chain Disruptions Task Force. Before her government service, Dr. Gorman spent nine years as Vice President of Responsible Leadership and Global Compliance at New Balance, giving her a rare ground-level perspective on how trade policy, tariffs, and supply chain risk play out in practice for U.S. manufacturers. She will be joined by Dr. Laura Taylor-Kale, Senior Fellow for Geoeconomics and Defense at the Council on Foreign Relations, who served as the first presidentially-appointed, Senate-confirmed Assistant Secretary of Defense for Industrial Base Policy from 2023 to 2025 — a role in which she led all defense industrial strategy and investments and authored the Pentagon's first-ever National Defense Industrial Strategy. Together, they bring a powerful combination of White House, Pentagon, Commerce Department, and private sector experience to bear on the defining industrial policy questions of our time.

title: PDW
Scaling Gap between Digital and Physical Platforms: Evidence from Fragmented Logistics Ecosystems
abstract:
Multimodal logistics – combining sea, air, rail, and road – accounts for 80% of global supply chains yet operates within profoundly fragmented landscapes. This fragmentation is physical, marked by disparate infrastructures; digital, characterized by incompatible systems; and regulatory, spanning conflicting national and international jurisdictions. While platforms have revolutionized asset-light digital industries, existing theories fail to account for the heavy assets and institutional constraints that define physical infrastructural needs in global trade, leaving a gap in understanding platform orchestration in logistics.
We address this by developing a scope-contingent framework for platform viability in fragmented markets. Employing the extended case method, we analyze the Port of Thessaloniki – a critical node in the Trans-European Transport Network – alongside global secondary evidence. Our analysis demonstrates that standard digital dominance logic is unattainable here; instead, viability depends on aligning platform architecture with operational scope. We posit three propositions: (i) local scopes favor innovation platforms acting as point solutions for specific infrastructure challenges; (ii) regional scopes require tightly coupled transaction platforms to manage flow matching, though they are constrained by divergent stakeholder objectives; and (iii) global scopes necessitate ecosystem platforms designed as "loosely coupled systems" to ensure interoperability across heterogeneous regulatory regimes. These findings offer implications for policy and management, shifting focus from digital scalability to robust architectures capable of navigating supply chain fragility and environmental imperatives.
authors: Kyungmin* (Brad) Lee (Salisbury University); Nitin Joglekar (Villanova University); Geoffrey Parker (Dartmouth College); Naoum Tsolakis (University of Cambridge)

title: Delivered on Demand: Uncovering the Value of On-Demand Delivery for Retail Success
abstract:
The rapid expansion of third-party on-demand delivery platforms has reshaped customer expectations for immediacy and introduced new complexities into retailers’ last-mile fulfillment systems. As a result, whether offering on-demand delivery enhances or undermines retailers’ performance remains an open question. This study examines how adopting third-party on-demand delivery affects retailers’ financial and operational performance and identifies which types of retailers benefit most from such partnerships. 
Our findings suggest that adopting third-party on-demand delivery generally improves retailers’ financial performance. Expanded customer access and enhanced convenience increase revenues, while operating costs also rise due to platform commissions and additional order-processing requirements. The net effect on profitability is positive because sales gains tend to outweigh cost increases. At the operational level, on-demand delivery reshapes inventory behavior rather than uniformly improving efficiency. Retailers adjust by holding higher inventory levels and incurring greater procurement costs to meet immediate fulfillment needs, resulting in largely stable inventory turnover despite higher sales volumes.
We further find substantial heterogeneity across retailers. Smaller retailers experience larger sales gains, likely because on-demand delivery reduces geographic frictions and compensates for limited physical presence. Larger retailers, by contrast, exhibit more muted revenue effects but manage cost increases more effectively, potentially due to scale advantages and established infrastructures. In addition, retailers that supplement platform-based delivery with private delivery capabilities achieve stronger financial and operational outcomes, suggesting that hybrid delivery models offer greater control over margins, service quality, and inventory flow.
Theoretically, this study fills a critical gap in the on-demand delivery literature by providing empirical evidence from the retail sector and extending existing insights to a context where inventory complexity and fulfillment heterogeneity differ fundamentally from restaurant settings. Managerially, the results highlight that the value of on-demand delivery depends not only on adoption but also on firm characteristics and delivery model design.
authors: Yawen Zheng* (The Ohio State University); Xiang Wan (The Ohio State University)

title: Achieving Rawlsian Justice in Food Rescue
abstract: We explore an implementable idea to optimize the fairness of food distribution (in a max-min sense) enabled by food rescue platforms. It is based on a close and ongoing collaboration with FoodRecovery.org (FR), which runs a two-sided platform nationwide where food donations are posted by organizations with surplus food and claimed on a first-come-first-serve (FCFS) basis by nonprofit organizations that serve communities in need. The matching between the donor and a recipient occurs automatically in FCFS fashion: Whoever claims the donated food first gets it. While operationally efficient and simple to execute, the FCFS matching raises fairness concerns, because it puts organizations that have more limited resources – thus slower response times – at a disadvantage. The optimal policy that maximizes the minimum “value” (e.g., pounds of food claimed, fraction of demand fulfilled) gives higher priority (thus more time to claim a donation) to recipients who have received less in the past and to those who have been slower in responding to FR’s notifications. We prove that this key insight can be codified into a simple index by which to rank-order eligible recipients. Our simulation models calibrated by real data from FR’s Florida operations confirm that this optimal policy leads to significantly more fair allocations than the existing FCFS allocation system.

session_name: AI and Data Tools for Manufacturing and Industry Intelligence
title: Beyond NAICS: A Generative AI Approach to Customized Industry Classification
abstract:
We present a novel approach that uses generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to identify and categorize the industries in which companies operate. Although standard industry classification systems such as the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) are widely used, many research questions do not fit neatly into their predefined categories. For example, the real estate development industry does not neatly fit into any single NAICS code or combination of NAICS codes. Instead, real estate developers are scattered across multiple NAICS codes, primarily in the real estate and construction sectors. This dynamic is not unique to real estate development or to NAICS; many industries of interest to researchers, practitioners, and policymakers are poorly captured by existing industry classification schemas. 

Conventional approaches to solving this problem rely on labor-intensive and costly data collection, cleaning, and validation processes, placing them out of reach for many small research teams and individual researchers. We demonstrate an alternative GenAI-enabled approach to customized industry classification and illustrate its application through a national landscape analysis of women-owned real estate development firms. We examine the representation of women-owned firms in the real estate development industry and compare their performance to that of other firms in the industry. 
By describing the methodology and illustrating its implementation, we show how publicly available GenAI models can be used to implement researcher-designed industry classifications with a high degree of accuracy and at substantially lower cost than conventional methods.
authors: Peter Eberhardt* (ICIC); Howard Wial (ICIC)

session_name: AI and Data Tools for Manufacturing and Industry Intelligence
title: The Real Bottleneck in AI: Power Generation, Environmental Policy, and National Competitiveness
abstract:
Artificial intelligence is framed as a central driver of productivity, industrial transformation, and national competitiveness. Policy discussions, however, continue to prioritize computer chips, data, and talent while underestimating the environmental and infrastructure constraints that shape AI scalability. This paper argues that the binding constraint on long-term AI competitiveness is not computational capacity alone, but the availability of low-cost, low-emissions power.

Building on prior work quantifying the environmental impact of datacenters that power AI, this study examines how rapidly scaling AI capacity influences energy demand and the resultant emissions by examining the current largest datacenter of xAI - The Colossus in Boxtown, TN. This paper explores the exponential growth of AI computational power, the resultant energy demand, emissions and current environmental policy.

The analysis demonstrates the need for cheap, low emission energy production is crucial to AI competitiveness and the bottleneck to scalability. Sustainable and affordable energy expansion—rather than the weakening of emissions standards—must be the central industrial policy lever for maintaining AI competitiveness in unprecedented times of AI innovation.
authors: Prathyaj Mantha* (PEER Consultants, P.C.)
category: Operations, Supply Chain, and AI-Enhanced Industry 4.0

session_name: AI and Data Tools for Manufacturing and Industry Intelligence
title: Manufacturing Intelligence Platform: Building Open Source Intelligence with Public Data
abstract: There are many useful public data sets that provide data and perspectives about regional manufacturing economies. However, these datasets operate at different scales, use different codes, and can be difficult to link together. As such, economic development stakeholders and industry practitioners are limited in their ability to operationalize public data to develop a clear picture about the composition, characteristics, and distribution of manufacturing activity in a particular region, or for a particular set of technologies. We have built an open source Manufacturing Intelligence Platform that aggregates and links public data about manufacturing in one location, allowing users without coding knowledge to investigate and explore public data about manufacturing activity. With this platform, users can get insights into how manufacturing activity differs across measurement sources, the composition of regional supply chains, and other features about regional manufacturing ecosystems. We discuss how this platform can help users develop better policies and interventions, and how generative AI tools can be used to link public datasets together and create informative dashboards about industry activity.
authors: Nikhil Kalathil* (Carnegie Mellon University)

title: Data Privacy Regulation in Digital Economy: Evidence from Mobile App Markets in Southeast and South Asia
abstract:
Privacy regulations have become a central policy instrument reshaping digital industries worldwide. Most advanced economies have widely adopted GDPR-style data protection laws, and emerging markets are increasingly adopting similar laws. However, while studies on privacy regulations focusing on advanced economies often take trust in formal institutions and enforceability for granted, little attention is paid to the weaker formal institutions and greater implementation uncertainties in emerging markets. Such differences fundamentally affect how privacy regulations affect consumers of digital services and industry dynamics.
We examine the market impact of tightening data privacy regulations in weak institutional environments. Specifically, by exploiting staggered policy promulgation and enactment across Southeast and South Asian countries that experienced rapid digital growth alongside expanding regulation, we examined the impact of these privacy laws on mobile app performance. Using 10 years of weekly data on 934 apps across 11 markets and multiple differences-in-difference (DiD) designs, we explore the causal effects of privacy laws on user behavior and app performance.
We show that, first, privacy regulation primarily operates on the extensive margin of digital participation. Following policy promulgation, app downloads decline by roughly 12-17%, install bases contract, and active users fall by about 6-7%. In contrast, intensive-margin indicators, such as time spent on apps, exhibit small or statistically insignificant changes. This pattern suggests that regulations mainly deter user participation as they raise users’ privacy awareness and concern under weak institutions, rather than offering assurance of privacy protection. Second, privacy regulations result in lower user experiences. Average user app ratings decline by approximately 0.15 points (on a scale of 5 points), and the volume of new ratings falls by 30-35% upon policy introduction. These rating responses precede most behavioral adjustments, indicating users’ reassessment of app trustworthiness or perceived value following heightened privacy awareness. Third, privacy regulations affect apps unevenly in that domestic apps and those with smaller prior user bases experience larger declines, while foreign apps and those with larger pre-existing user bases remain resilient. These patterns point to differences in compliance capacity and perceived credibility, implying that privacy regulation in low-trust environments may unintentionally reinforce market concentration and disadvantage domestic and smaller developers.
Taken together, our findings contribute to studies of digital privacy rights and highlight a central trade-off in privacy policy under weak institutions. While data protection strengthens individuals’ ownership over personal data, it also reduces digital participation and shifts market share toward already advantaged firms from advanced economies. For firms in emerging markets, this underscores the importance of complementary measures, such as credible enforcement and transparency, to acknowledge the value of users’ data and ensure users’ trust in firms’ compliance.
authors: Mingtao Xu (Tsinghua University); Wenzhe Xu* (Tsinghua University)

title: The Co-Evolution of Policy Framework and the Artificial Intelligence Innovation Ecosystem in Taiwan
abstract: How do innovation ecosystems evolve in response to global technological shifts and institutional adaptation? How does the high-tech sector in small emerging economies engage with the global innovation ecosystem? This study investigates the transformation of the artificial intelligence (AI) innovation ecosystem in Taiwan, examining how firms engage in knowledge exchange, comply with international regulations, and adapt to industrial restructuring. Adopting a multi-level perspective (MLP) as the framework, we analyze the dynamic interactions between technological niches, regimes, and landscapes. Combining scientometric mapping, social network analysis (SNA), and qualitative system dynamics to trace knowledge flows, collaboration patterns, and policy feedback loops from 2000 to 2023. The findings reveal that while Taiwan’s AI ecosystem is deeply integrated into global knowledge networks—particularly in semiconductor and biomedical domains—it faces a structural asymmetry. Firms leverage their established hardware strengths but rely heavily on strategic partnerships with global technology leaders to compensate for deficiencies in software and algorithms. Consequently, despite strong global connectivity, the sector struggles to establish a distinctive niche beyond its traditional manufacturing dominance. This study contributes to the innovation systems literature by integrating qualitative system dynamics into the MLP framework, thereby mapping policy-innovation feedback loops in small open economies. The findings provide critical insights for policymakers on managing ecosystem transitions and for firms on developing competitive business models to bridge the "hardware-software divide" in the global AI economy.
authors: Shih-Hsin Chen (Institute of Technology of Management, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, ASU Barrett & O’connor Washington Center); Hung-Chi Chang* (National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University)

title: The Mutual Shaping of the Policies and Sectoral Developments in AI-Enabled Biomedical  Clusters: A Comparative Prospective of Responsible Innovation in Taiwan and Virginia
abstract: How can responsible innovation reshape the development and governance of AI-enabled biomedical technology in different socio-technical contexts? This research explores how responsible innovation can be situated in different socio-political contexts. Biomedical technology was selected as the focal domain in metropolitan DC in the United States (US) and Taiwan. This study investigates how responsible innovation principles are interpreted, implemented, and negotiated within biomedical innovation practices. Semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders (n=46), 23 in Taiwan and 23 in US, policy documents, and official reports provide empirical data for the case studies. The U.S. system emphasizes market responsiveness and reflexivity, driven by investor pressures and entrepreneurial dynamics, whereas Taiwan’s mission-oriented governance cultivates future-oriented strategies shaped by adaptive policy frameworks and international markets. Nevertheless, in both systems, patients remain peripheral in the early stages of innovation, and hospitals tend to function primarily as clinical trial sites rather than as co-creators of innovative technologies. The level of commitment to RI is insufficient to embed social values in the process or healthcare outcomes in both cases. This study contributes to a more context-sensitive understanding of responsible innovation and offers insights into assessing regional innovation.
authors: Rider W. Foley (Department of Engineering & Society, School of Engineering and Applied Science, University of Virginia); Shih-Hsin Chen* (Institute of Technology of Management, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, ASU Barrett & O’connor Washington Center); Wen-Hsin Chi (Institute of Technology of Management, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University; Department of Engineering & Society, School of Engineering and Applied Science, University of Virginia); Hung-Chi Chang (National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University)

title: Forecasting the Winners and Losers of H-1B Reforms Across Industries and Workers: Will firms, universities, and health care lose workers or profits?
abstract: As the U.S.’s largest skilled guestworker program, the H-1B visa is used by tens of thousands of firms who employ more than 600 thousand of these guestworkers. The H-1B program has been described as the swiss army knife of guest worker programs because of the varied nature of employers and workers who use it. The Trump administration proposing the most farreaching reforms to the H-1B program since its inception. The three reforms implemented for this year are: 1) employers are assessed a new $100,000 fee for visas for certain workers, 2) the annual process for selecting new visas has been modified to favor higher wages, and 3) stepped up enforcement of program rules by the Department of Labor (DOL) . The DOL has also announced changes the minimum wage employers are required to pay H-1B workers. These reforms will alter the types of firms that apply for and receive visas, and the pool of worker-beneficiaries. We examine the expected winners and losers from these policy changes and potential impact, with focus  on the tech sector as the largest user of this guestworker visa and health care system which relies on the H-1B for a large supply of residents.
authors: Ron Hira* (Howard University); Hal Salzman (Rutgers University)

session_name: Taking Stock: System Dynamics Modeling in Industry Studies
title: Managing Capacity for Electric Vehicle Batteries Recycling
abstract: Recycling electric vehicle (EV) batteries is essential for reducing reliance on virgin raw materials, and proper planning of recycling capacity is necessary. Recycling facilities rely on two main sources of feedstock – used batteries from retired EVs and production scrap from manufacturing of batteries for new EVs. Currently, due to the limited installed base of EVs, the supply of used batteries is low, but is expected to increase as more EVs are sold. Conversely, production scrap is currently high but is bound to decrease within the next few years as manufacturing processes mature. Balancing these two trends is important to maintain sufficient recycling capacity and its efficient utilization. Although optimistic EV sales projections created significant expansion of battery production and recycling facilities in the last few years, recent consumer hesitancy and announcements from OEMs to slow or pause EV production suggest a substantially lower EV sales growth trajectory vs. earlier estimates. Consequently, not only EV battery production may experience an "overshoot-and-collapse" dynamic, but future flows of used EV batteries will decrease, leading to periods of underutilized recycling capacity and reduced demand for recycled materials. We use a fully calibrated model of the U.S. vehicle fleet to explore the feedback between trajectories of EV sales, EV battery production, and recycling capacity, focusing on optimal recycling capacity planning. Our findings offer strategic insights for vehicle OEMs, battery manufacturers, and recyclers to establish robust and resilient operational policies for EV battery recycling.
authors: Sergey Naumov* (Pennsylvania State University)

session_name: Taking Stock: System Dynamics Modeling in Industry Studies
title: Cartels, Policy, and Technological Substitution: What the history of the Synthetic Rubber Industry Can Teach Us About the Rare Earths Supply Chain
abstract: Rare earth elements are critical inputs to sustainability, defense, and a wide range of other advanced technologies, yet their supply chains remain highly concentrated and vulnerable to disruption. In this presentation, we draw lessons from the twentieth-century history of the U.S. synthetic rubber industry to illuminate the dynamics shaping contemporary rare earth supply chains. Revisiting the longer arc of synthetic rubber development, we use a system dynamics approach to show how cartel power, policy intervention, and technological substitution repeatedly interacted to produce cycles of supply restriction, capacity expansion, and innovation. We then examine how these historical dynamics map onto today's rare earth supply chains and the policy challenges they pose. Concentrated processing capacity controlled by regional cartels, together with growing industry interest in reshoring capacity, material substitution, and design-based workarounds, closely mirrors the forces observed in the rubber industry. U.S. policy interventions can support industry efforts to reduce dependence on cartel power across the rare earth supply chain—from extraction and refining to midstream products such as permanent magnets. At the same time, cartel-controlled suppliers may act strategically to deter or undermine private investment, further complicating policy responses and underscoring the need for adaptive, evolving policy approaches. We conclude by discussing implications for theory, managerial decision-making, and public policy in this critical domain.
authors: Edward Anderson* (University of Texas at Austin), Sergey Naumov (Pennsylvania State University), Burcu Tan (University of New Mexico), Robert Benny (University of Texas at Austin)

session_name: Taking Stock: System Dynamics Modeling in Industry Studies
title: Doubling Down on Dual-Fuels: Heat Pump and Fossil Backups' Effects on Grid Load, Cost, and Emissions in Massachusetts
abstract: Heat pumps (HPs) are a key technology to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and many governments offer HP rebates funded by utility ratepayers. However, rising electricity bills increase pressure to reduce rebates, and adoption may exacerbate winter peak electricity demand when HPs are least efficient. Dual-fuel systems are one proposed solution: they usually utilize a heat pump but use a fossil fuel backup in cold periods, lowering grid load. Moreover, heat pumps in these systems can have less capacity, limiting installation costs and allowing for lower rebates. We develop a system dynamics model of heating system purchases. The model distinguishes between homeowners replacing a broken system or reconsidering a functioning one. Homeowners consider both operating and installation costs, and those with functioning systems can retain them as backups to limit dual-fuels' incremental costs. The model is calibrated to Massachusetts, a cold-climate state with ambitious HP adoption targets. We find rebates for dual-fuel systems reduce peak load but increase emissions and subsidy outlays. Because homeowners can keep existing systems as backups, dual-fuels are popular with low rebates and increasing subsidies causes nearly all HPs to be dual-fuels, raising outlays and emissions from backups. Conversely, shifting rebate levels to all-electric systems lowers emissions with minimal change in outlays – but raises peak demand. Our results suggest limiting rebates for dual-fuel systems and complementing all-electric HP rebates with demand-side policies, such as energy efficiency incentives. More broadly, our work highlights that installed base effects can amplify the unintended fiscal and environmental consequences of technology subsidies.
authors: Alexander Kuptel* (MIT Sloan School of Management), John Sterman (MIT Sloan School of Management)

title: Break
When Rareness and Scarcity Interact: Complementary, Substitution, and Conflicting Effects in Resource-Based Competitive Advantage
abstract: Resource-based theory has long held that resources must be limited in supply to generate competitive advantage. Two distinct traditions emerged—Barney’s emphasis on rareness (the degree to which a resource is possessed by few competing firms) and Peteraf’s emphasis on scarcity (the degree to which aggregate demand exceeds available supply)—which Peteraf and Barney (2003) reconciled as “very nearly the same.” While this phrasing left conceptual space for differences, subsequent literature has often treated rareness and scarcity as completely interchangeable. We refine this reconciliation by showing that while functionally similar, rareness and scarcity operate through sufficiently distinct mechanisms that their interaction creates dynamics interchangeability cannot predict. When resources exhibit both characteristics, three patterns emerge: complementary (mechanisms amplify advantage beyond additive effects), substitution (context determines dominance), and conflicting (mechanisms work at cross-purposes—differentiation creating unfulfillable demand, scarcity preventing network effects, or resource allocation dilemmas reducing net advantage below either alone). Conflicts indicate mechanistic distinction within functional similarity, as identical concepts cannot conflict. We specify boundary conditions determining patterns and examine how resource origins (exogenous versus endogenous) moderate strategic flexibility. Our framework refines Peteraf and Barney’s reconciliation: functional similarity dominates when one mechanism operates; mechanistic distinctions require specification when both operate simultaneously.
authors: Temitope Oladimeji* (University of Massachusetts Amherst)

title: The Habitable Zone of Scientific Creativity: Cognitive Distance, Absorptive Capacity, and Impact
abstract: Originality is widely viewed as a driver of scientific progress, yet evidence on how novelty translates into impact remains mixed. Prior studies emphasize recombination benefits but often overlook how the scientific system’s capacity to interpret novel ideas changes over time. Using 23.1 million life-science articles published between 1824 and 2025, this study examines how disciplinary originality—measured as Average Interdisciplinary Distance (AID)—shapes scientific impact across historical periods. We find a robust inverted-U relationship: moderate disciplinary distance maximizes citations, while both conventional and highly distant work is less influential. Crucially, this relationship is historically dynamic. During the post-war Big Science era, the range of impactful originality broadened, whereas in the digital era it narrowed and became more selective despite high peak impact. These findings show that originality is rewarded only within historically contingent “habitable zones” defined by the scientific system’s collective absorptive capacity. The study contributes to innovation research by linking recombination, absorptive capacity, and long-run structural change in science.
authors: Tan Tran* (Beyondegrees Sas); Christian Goglin (ICD Business School)

title: Latent Hazards: Counterperformative Effects of Certification in New Ventures
abstract: New firms invest heavily in legitimacy to mobilize stakeholder resources. Consistent with institutional theory, certification is widely argued, and empirically shown, to confer legitimacy and unlock resources from wary audiences. Yet we know far less about when certification can backfire, especially for young ventures. I investigate how certifications can constrain the very resources they were meant to enhance, a process I call certification counterperformativity. Using a qualitative embedded case study of ethical certifications in the cosmetics industry, I illustrate how certifications can embed latent hazards that remain largely invisible at adoption but later become consequential when firms attempt to innovate, scale, expand geographically, or respond to shifting market expectations. Through a thematic analysis of interviews, fieldwork, archival documents, and public statements from informants positioned along the product value chain, I develop a process model explaining how latent hazards (internal friction, operational strain, and strategic rigidity) are activated by subsequent firm initiatives and/or external shifts in standards, stakeholder preferences, and certification governance. Once activated, these hazards generate counterperformative outcomes that can erode flexibility, slow execution, and narrow strategic options, thereby undermining the very legitimacy and resource access certification initially helped secure. In doing so, I primarily contribute to certification research by theorizing certification not only as a legitimacy mechanism, but also as a potential source of deferred constraint, clarifying how and when an apparently beneficial signal can turn into a binding liability for new ventures. Second, as a tertiary contribution, this study contributes to entrepreneurship research by reframing early legitimacy-seeking as an intertemporal strategic tradeoff, showing how decisions made to secure external validation can introduce path dependencies that shape and potentially constrain new ventures’ future strategic trajectories.
authors: Scott Taylor* (University of Southern California)

title: Multimodal Optimal Distinctiveness
abstract:
How do entrepreneurs convey the distinctiveness of their ventures without compromising categorical comprehension? Drawing on optimal distinctiveness and multimodality studies, we introduce the concept of “multimodal optimal distinctiveness” and theorize how visual and verbal modes serve complementary functions that jointly help entrepreneurs achieve optimal distinctiveness. Analyzing data from over 140,000 Kickstarter campaigns and employing state-of-the-art foundation models, we find that visual distinctiveness (conformity) negatively (positively) relates to funding outcomes, while verbal distinctiveness positively relates to funding outcomes. Moreover, the positive effect of verbal distinctiveness is strongest when visual distinctiveness is low, suggesting that modalities serve complementary functions—visuals anchor category comprehension while text articulates differentiation. 

We further examine how category heterogeneity—the variance of distinctiveness within a category—moderates these relationships. In homogeneous categories where prototypes are well-defined, verbal distinctiveness shows a monotonically positive effect; the category itself serves as an evaluation anchor. In heterogeneous categories where audience expectations are diffuse, verbal distinctiveness exhibits a U-shaped pattern: moderate distinctiveness underperforms relative to either strong conformity or bold differentiation. These findings suggest that the conformity-distinctiveness trade-off is contingent on the strength of categorical anchors available to audiences.              

Our findings advance a multimodal view of optimal distinctiveness in which different modalities are not interchangeable but complementary in satisfying the dual needs for fitting in and standing out. Our study suggests that the conformity-distinctiveness trade-off need not be a balancing act but rather a design problem that can be resolved through strategic deployment of cultural means across modalities.
authors: Rui Wang* (Tsinghua University); Joel Gehman (George Washington University)

title: Lean Thinking, Deep Impact?  Early Exploration Strategies and Commercialization of Deeptech Ventures
abstract:
This paper examines how early exploration strategies, sequential or parallel, shape the financial and innovation trajectories of deeptech ventures. These firms must navigate multiple dimensions of uncertainty, including technological feasibility. Moreover, they rely on physical assets to commercialize, making exploration costly. Prior research on entrepreneurial strategy emphasizes experimentation to resolve uncertainty but largely focuses on asset-light settings such as software. Even lean startup methods, which encourage early commercial exploration, are better suited to digital ventures where uncertainty is primarily market-based. Consequently, less is known about the implications of exploration strategy in high-uncertainty, asset-intensive environments. I assembled a novel longitudinal dataset of 13,790 hardware-oriented ventures using primary and archival sources, augmented by machine learning and NLP. Employing multiple empirical strategies, including an exogenous technological development (3D printing), the study finds that parallel exploration improves early commercial outcomes by accelerating market learning and mitigating information frictions, yet risks premature technological lock-in. In contrast, sequential exploration fosters deeper learning, yielding long-run financial and innovation performance.
These results highlight the trade-offs faced by boundedly rational entrepreneurs as they balance resolving uncertainty with enhancing organizational learning. The study extends research on entrepreneurial strategy and experimentation to asset-intensive contexts and delineates the boundary conditions under which lean methods are effective in scaling science and technology ventures.
authors: Vinay Subramanian* (Wharton)

title: Service Design and Innovation for Aging Societies: Introducing Silver Prosperity Index (SPI)
abstract: This paper presents the Silver Prosperity Index (SPI), a data-driven framework for evaluating service innovation in aging societies. The SPI is structured around four pillars: Economic Empowerment, Health and Well-being, Social Cohesion and Connectivity, and Security and Protection. It integrates primary survey data with secondary datasets, applying standardized normalization, confirmatory factor weighting, and cross-validation to ensure reliability. A 2025 application across all 50 U.S. states demonstrates its ability to generate detailed, localized insights. Results demonstrate significant regional disparities in support for aging populations, particularly in digital access, workforce participation, and community resilience. These gaps signal opportunities for developing innovative services targeting older adults.
authors: Rohit Verma* (University of South Carolina), Kejia Hu (University of Oxford), Xin Ding (Rutgers University), and Diep Pham (University of South Carolina)

title: Cascading Failures: An Analysis of a Major IT Outage
abstract:
(a) Purpose: Modern operations rely on tightly integrated digital systems that enable efficiency but also create new forms of interdependence. When one firm’s technology fails, the consequences can cascade across others that share physical infrastructure. This study examines how such IT disruptions propagate through shared operational resources. By doing so, we unpack both the direct effect and the spillover effects of IT disruptions on firms’ operations. Our empirical analyses contribute to the literature by offering a comprehensive understanding of the consequences of IT disruptions. Furthermore, the findings inform firms—including those not directly affected—of the collateral damages associated with the increasing frequency of IT disruptions in recent years.

(b) Research Method: We leverage the global CrowdStrike outage of 2024 as a natural experiment in the U.S. airline industry, where some carriers experienced operational paralysis while others remained functional due to differences in their IT vendors. Airlines whose IT systems failed are referred to as disrupted airlines, while airlines whose systems remained functional but share airport resources with disrupted carriers are referred to as collateral airlines. This variation in exposure allows us to identify how a focal firm’s disruption spills over to others through shared resources such as gates, runways, and departure slots, and how the magnitude of these spillovers depends on the disrupted firm’s degree of control over shared operational infrastructure.
Using operational data from U.S. airlines, we estimate the impact of the outage on flight on-time performance. The analysis applies a difference-in-differences framework that treats the IT outage as an external shock to airlines’ operations. The observation window is divided into an 18-day pre-treatment period and a 20-day post-treatment period. To mitigate selection concerns, we employ propensity score matching to pair routes in the treatment and control groups. Flights of airlines operating at airports with minimal presence of disrupted carriers serve as the control group.

(c) Findings: The results show that while the IT outage increased delays for both disrupted and collateral airlines, the impact was substantially larger for the disrupted carrier. For disrupted airlines, delays were more severe at non-hub airports, suggesting that at major hubs they could draw on additional gates, ground crews, and scheduling flexibility to restore operations. For collateral airlines, delays were more severe at airports where they shared hubs with disrupted airlines, likely due to the disrupted carrier’s intensive recovery efforts that strained shared resources.
Dynamic analyses reveal a sharp and short-run surge in delays for disrupted carriers, peaking in the first week and easing afterward. In contrast, collateral carriers experienced a milder negative impact but took longer to return to normal operations. This pattern suggests that disrupted airlines are more motivated and better positioned to secure resources during recovery.

(d) Implications: The findings demonstrate that shared infrastructure can turn a single firm’s disruption into a collective operational problem. When multiple firms depend on common resources, recovery efforts by one can restrict access for others, creating prolonged collateral damage. These insights highlight the importance of coordinated recovery planning, transparency, and resource-sharing protocols to mitigate the broader impacts of large-scale IT failures.

title: The Financial Impact of Supply Chains
abstract: Using extensive financial data and visualization, we discover a critical but subtle connection among supply chain operations, financial performance and stock market valuation for a broad range of industries and countries. The robust discovery indicates that a small change in supply chain operations can be translated into a big impact on the financials and market values for a majority of industry sectors in the US and beyond. The discovery may significantly expand the out-reach of the supply chain management field by answering the question that most students and practitioners have before entering this field: how do supply chains impact companies' financials and stock market performance? The discovery can also guide companies in their operations to improve shareholder value.
authors: Yao Zhao* (Rutgers University)

title: Learning curve effects in outsourcing: Evidence from the medtech industry
abstract: Contract manufacturing in the medtech industry has been observed to grow at a pace about twice as fast as the medtech industry overall. Against this backdrop and considering the health and safety implications of the industry for the general public, it is crucial to understand how outsourcing can be successfully managed. However, unlike the case of pharmaceutical manufacturing, little data is publicly available despite oversight by the same regulatory bodies, such as the FDA. Therefore, we draw on two decades' worth of unique panel data on subassemblies of high-runner medical devices of an industrial company. To study the quality dynamics following outsourcing, we employ a quasi-experimental setup investigating the development in spare-part requirements across the lifetime of devices for subassemblies relocated to be outsourced at one point in time, relative to comparable subassemblies that were relocated in-house at the same time. In particular, we focus on the analysis of learning curve effects and hypothesize how product and process complexity affect the learning curve of contract manufacturers.
authors: Ilkim Güneri (ETH Zurich); Oliver Von Dzengelevski* (ETH Zurich); John Gray (The Ohio State University); Torbjorn Netland (ETH Zurich)

title: From Persuasion to Learning: Dynamic Information Design in Supply Chains
abstract:
Problem definition: We study information design in a supply chain where information sharing affects not only current operational decisions but also future forecast accuracy and execution outcomes. In a retailer–supplier setting with mismatch costs, the retailer can share data to improve the supplier’s demand forecast and disclose information to influence the supplier’s production decision. 

Academic/practical relevance: Most information design models treat payoff functions as fixed and study disclosure in static environments. In practice, however, data sharing improves forecasting capability over time and alters how operational decisions are executed. Understanding how learning and implementation frictions interact with information disclosure is critical for designing effective data-sharing policies in modern supply chains. 

Methodology: We develop a stylized analytical model of supply chain information design with endogenous forecast learning and execution reliability. Data sharing increases forecast precision over time, reshaping the induced mismatch cost function faced by the retailer. We characterize optimal disclosure and data-sharing policies using Bayesian persuasion techniques, comparative statics, and dynamic analysis. 

Results: We show that forecast learning flattens the induced mismatch cost function, reducing the value of manual belief manipulation and substituting data sharing for traditional disclosure. As a result, information sharing can be optimal even when it is myopically costly. We further show that execution reliability amplifies the operational value of learning by strengthening the link between forecast precision and realized decisions, increasing both static and intertemporal incentives for data sharing. These mechanisms generate disclosure patterns that differ sharply from static information design benchmarks. 

Managerial implications: Our results suggest that investments in forecasting and execution capabilities fundamentally change optimal information-sharing policies. As learning improves, firms should rely less on selective disclosure and more on data sharing. Moreover, the value of sharing data depends critically on execution reliability: improving forecasting without the ability to act on forecasts may yield limited benefits.
authors: Shailesh Divey* (The Ohio State University)

title: Optimal Design of Reliability Rating Systems and Resource Allocation for Improving Drug Shortages
abstract:
Generic drug shortages have been a persistent issue the U.S., compromising public health.
A primary driver of these shortages is a fundamental market failure; because generic drugs are viewed as undifferentiated commodities, the market prioritizes the lowest price over long-term reliable supply. Such price-driven competition discourages manufacturers from investing in reliability. To address this systemic failure, U.S. policymakers have initiated two independent regulatory moves: the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) Quality Management Maturity (QMM) program, designed to rate manufacturing quality to facilitate market differentiation, and the Senate Finance Committee’s proposed Medicare Drug Shortage Prevention and Mitigation Program, which would leverage tiered financial incentives.

Despite their shared objectives, these frameworks currently lack a cohesive economic integration. This study utilizes a game-theoretic model to analyze the optimal design of discretized reliability rating systems and the strategic allocation of resources between two suppliers with asymmetric reliability capabilities. Our results indicate that when a policymaker can override firm decisions to maximize total expected supply (conditional on firm profitability), resources should be prioritized for the less capable supplier. Conversely, when firms maintain autonomous decision-making, optimal resource allocation must shift toward the more capable supplier to ensure the market rewards the highest tiers of reliability. Paradoxically, we demonstrate that the optimal resource allocation for the high-capability supplier may increase and then decrease as its competitor’s capability diminishes. This research provides actionable insights and theoretical guidelines for integrating quality-based regulatory assessments and with the financial incentive reforms currently under consideration.
authors: Junghee Lee* (University of Notre Dame); Eojin Han (University of Notre Dame)

title: "If we don't do it, who will?" Stretching humanitarian operations capabilities in the West Africa Ebola epidemic
abstract: The West Africa Ebola response in March 2014 was an extremely challenging emergency for the humanitarian community. Few humanitarian organizations were prepared for its complexity, but they stretched their capabilities to respond when the urgent need became clear. Through an in-depth case study of one organization's Ebola response, this paper explores the limits of humanitarian operational systems and processes in novel contexts and examines how they adapt to meet operational needs. We find that some operational processes were not flexible enough to meet the needs of the response. The resulting operational challenges were solved at least as often by individuals stepping up to find solutions as by changing the organization's official processes. Humanitarian organizations should recognize the importance of individual efforts by response staff in adapting processes to novel needs, and should consider developing more flexible processes. Our findings demonstrate the importance of individual knowledge and initiative when organizational systems and processes are stretched to their limits.
authors: Lauren Bateman (George Washington University); Erica Gralla* (George Washington University)

title: Rewiring the humanitarian ecosystem: relationships in a post-USAID world
abstract: The substantial reductions in USAID  funding have created unprecedented challenges for organizations across the humanitarian and development sectors. While much attention has focused on programmatic impacts (i.e. number of grants and programs cancelled), there has been limited systematic research on how these disruptions have affected the complex web of relationships that enable effective humanitarian and development work – relationships between implementers, suppliers, government agencies, and those served by aid. Our research aims to fill this critical knowledge gap by examining changes across the aid ecosystem. We deployed an anonymous survey of humanitarian professionals focused on six key areas: partnerships and collaboration, information and knowledge access, financial and organizational stability, internal organizational dynamics, supply chain and logistics, and programmatic service delivery. A series of in-depth interviews supplement the quantitative data to identify how cuts have been felt by organizations and those they serve. The findings show differences in the impact of cuts across geographic and organizational lines, surface key weaknesses and strengths in the evolving aid ecosystem, and highlight some positive adaptations along with many negative impacts.
authors: Maryam Deloffre (George Washington University); Caitlin Grady (George Washington University); Erica Gralla* (George Washington University)

title: A Theoretical Framework for Teaching STEM Graduate Students Entrepreneurship, Family Business Governance, and Scaling to Global Family Conglomerates
abstract: During this study, I conducted a systematic literature review to develop a comprehensive theoretical framework for teaching entrepreneurship to Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) students. Drawing upon the theoretical foundations of Experiential Learning Theory (Kolb, 1984), Constructivist Theory (Piaget, 1971; Vygotsky, 1978), Cognitivism Theory (Bruner, 1966; 1971), Social Identity Theory (Tajfel et al., 1979), Achievement Motivation Theory (McClelland, 1961; 1976), Theory of Economic Development (Schumpeter, 1934; 1942), Human Capital Theory (Becker, 1976; 1993), and Expectancy Theory (Vroom, 1964), the study synthesizes interdisciplinary perspectives from education, psychology, economics, and entrepreneurship. The integration of entrepreneurship and STEM education has become a critical and rapidly evolving area of scholarship, necessitating a comprehensive review from multiple perspectives (Yu et al., 2025). At the micro level, entrepreneurial career development describes the process by which individuals perceive entrepreneurship as a meaningful professional pathway (Ozyazici et al., 2025), emphasizing the transferability of STEM competencies such as problem decomposition, analytical reasoning, and innovation to entrepreneurial contexts. The proposed framework prioritizes experiential, cognitively scaffolded, and socially embedded learning approaches that foster the development of an entrepreneurial mindset, strategic thinking, governance competence, and emotional maturity. In alignment with the academy’s mission to advance knowledge and demonstrate societal value, this study contributes to the fields of entrepreneurship and family business management by presenting a theoretically grounded framework for teaching STEM graduate students’ entrepreneurship, family business governance, and the scaling of Global Family Conglomerates.
authors: John Lecounte* (St John Fisher University )

title: Political Entrepreneurs: Are Entrepreneurs in Politics Entrepreneurial in Policymaking?
abstract: Business interests influence public policy through lobbying and campaign contributions, yet business owners can also shape policy by entering elected office themselves. How does entrepreneurial experience shape policymaking once entrepreneurs become legislators? This paper examines whether entrepreneurs in legislative office behave differently from other legislators and whether they advance broad business interests or a distinct entrepreneurial policy agenda. We construct a novel dataset linking personal financial disclosures of state legislators to comprehensive legislative records from 26 U.S. states between 2009 and 2023. Using detailed information on business ownership and employment, we identify legislators with entrepreneurial backgrounds and link them to the bills they sponsor. Applying large language models to bill texts, we classify legislation as pro-business or pro-entry and measure the volume, share, and intensity of such bills. We further benchmark legislative agendas using bills supported by state Chambers of Commerce. We find that entrepreneurial representation varies primarily across states and is negatively associated with legislative professionalism and state-level entrepreneurial activity, consistent with the idea that opportunity costs discourage entrepreneurs from holding office. Once elected, entrepreneurs are not more prolific sponsors overall but are significantly more likely to initiate legislation as first primary sponsors. They also do not act as broad representatives of business interests; instead, they selectively advance pro-entry policies, focusing on antitrust and deregulation. These findings highlight an insider channel of political engagement of business interests and show how entrepreneurial experience shapes legislative agenda by targeting barriers to market entry rather than advancing generic pro-business issues.
authors: Joyce Ma* (The Fuqua School of Business, Duke University); Aaron Chatterji (The Fuqua School of Business, Duke University); Jorge  Guzman (Columbia Business School, Columbia University); Ryan Mcdevitt (The Fuqua School of Business, Duke University)

title: Mapping the Evolution of Entrepreneurship as a Scientific Discipline: A Sixty-Year Bibliometric and Network Analysis (1960–2020)
abstract:
This study examines the evolution and consolidation of entrepreneurship as a scientific discipline through a comprehensive bibliometric and network analysis of publications indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database between 1960 and 2020. The dataset comprises 76,448 cleaned and validated records after filtering an initial sample of 144,861 documents that included articles, proceedings, and meeting papers. The analysis quantifies scientific productivity, disciplinary intersections, and co-authorship dynamics across six decades.
The findings show that entrepreneurship has progressively evolved from a marginal topic in economics and business toward a multidisciplinary domain connected to over 120 research areas, including engineering, education, environmental sciences, and emerging fields such as medical ethics and sports sciences. The United States, China, and the United Kingdom are identified as the most prolific contributors. Network visualizations reveal a growing density of collaborations, particularly after 2000, when the co-authorship network exhibits clear consolidation and the emergence of large, interconnected research communities.
Three econometric models were estimated to assess the influence of network characteristics on individual researchers’ productivity and impact. The results indicate that both the number of distinct co-authors (degree) and the frequency of repeated collaborations have significant positive effects on publication output and citations, while centrality measures (betweenness and eigenvector) show differentiated relationships with productivity and impact. The study confirms the cumulative and collaborative nature of scientific knowledge in entrepreneurship and highlights the critical role of sustained co-authorship in shaping the field’s global research structure.
authors: Claudia Gonzalez Brambila* (ITAM)

title: Resource Redeployment in Entrepreneurial Firms: A Theoretical Model and Empirical Evidence from the Oil-drilling Industry
abstract: Resource redeployment is a resource allocation strategy, or a real option, which involves withdrawing resources from one use and allocating them to another use. Such redeployment was elaborated conceptually and studied empirically. Meanwhile, three serious issues remained unresolved in research. First, research on resource redeployment was restricted to large established (and mostly multi-business) firms, which were even believed to be unique in having the option to redeploy their resources. However, entrepreneurial firms are under strong pressure to efficiently allocate resources, and resource redeployment is one of important strategies to do so. Second, empirical research on resource redeployment never registered it directly. Instead, either some circumstantial evidence was used to operationalize resource redeployment in the available data or the observed choices could not clearly separate resource redeployment from other resource allocation strategies. Finally, the effect of uncertainty, the key determinant of the redeployment option, was poorly understood. On the one hand formal models predicted that the value of the redeployment option is enhanced by uncertainty. On the other hand, verbal theoretical accounts referred to hysteresis present in real options and predicted that such hysteresis results in the negative effect of uncertainty on the use of the redeployment option. This study uses a large sample of entrepreneurial ventures that operate in oil-drilling industry in Texas and can redeploy their rigs across oil fields. The empirical analysis demonstrates that resource redeployment is very prevalent among such firms. In addition to registering redeployment directly, this study empirically relates it to formal predictions of what determines it, including uncertainty.
authors: Arkadiy Sakhartov* (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign); Toby Li (Texas A&M University); Jeffrey Reuer (Purdue University)

title: Potential Impact of Tariffs on the Price of Generic Drugs Made in the US with Imported Active Ingredients
abstract: Using U.S. importation data 2019-2024, this study modeled the potential impact of tariffs on the prices of generic drugs manufactured in the U.S. with imported active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs). Under baseline assumptions a 100% worldwide tariff would result in average price increase of 30% (additional $21.15) per prescription and a blended tariff based on rates proposed by the Federal Administration would result in an average price increase of 10% (additional $6.22) per prescription for domestically-produced generics using imported APIs. Estimates varied across drugs reflecting different API importation patterns. Assumptions on the tariff rate, the contribution of the API cost to the final drug price, and on the supply chain’s ability to absorb the added tariff cost contributed markedly to determining the final price. The study findings do not generalize to U.S.-made generics using U.S.-made API but could be relevant to U.S.-made branded drugs using imported API. Tariffs could raise costs for U.S. drug manufacturers using imported APIs, potentially limiting affordability and manufacturers’ competitiveness in U.S. and global markets. Policies to incentivize “made-in-America” prescription drugs should incentivize domestic API production or reconsider API tariffs.

title: From Bribes to Bytes: How Has Fraud Evolved in the U.S. Transportation Sector Projects?
abstract: The United States transportation infrastructure sector is currently navigating a period of historic capital expansion, a context that historical data suggests is frequently correlated with opportunistic behavior and systemic fraud. This study presents a longitudinal analysis of 2,028 confirmed Department of Transportation (DOT) violations spanning from 1998 to 2025. Transitioning beyond traditional statistical methods, this research employs Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) to deconstruct the linguistic architecture of fraud descriptions, enabling a high-precision classification of latent project governance failures. The analysis reveals a distinct "Digital Crossover," where physical bribery and safety non-compliance have been superseded by digital wire fraud and complex "pass-through" schemes involving Disadvantaged Business Enterprises (DBE). Furthermore, semantic clustering identifies five major frauds, with "DBE Shell Games" and "Moving Hostage Schemes" carrying the highest financial severity. The paper prposes a transition from retrospective auditing to real-time, blockchain-enabled "Verify-then-Pay" frameworks to close the verification gap in project delivery.
authors: Young Kwak* (George Washington University); Manisha Bhetwal (George Washington University); Sureewan  Jampathong (George Washington University)

title: Volume or Depth? Operational Pathways to Federal Funding Success in Nonprofits
abstract:
Project grants and cooperative agreements constitute nearly one-third of total government funding for nonprofit organizations (NPOs) in the U.S. However, given frequent funding reductions, NPOs face increasing pressure to configure their operational competencies to match the distinct requirements of federal agencies. Because project grants require standardized competencies while cooperative agreements demand collaborative, agency-specific ones, NPOs must strategically choose between two operational pathways: volume (pursuing funding across multiple agencies) or depth (building repetitive funding interactions with the same agency). This study examines how these pathways shape NPOs' ability to signal the required competencies to secure future federal funding.
We assemble a unique longitudinal dataset of 7,845 federal awards totaling $15.8 billion to 1,925 NPOs from 2017–2024 and apply Relational Event Models to capture the temporal dependence among sequential funding events. Our results show that the success of an NPO’s operational pathway depends critically on the funding mechanism. Depth pathways in project grants strengthen relationships with federal agencies and increase the likelihood of securing both awards types (project grants and cooperative agreements) by up to 2.5%. In contrast, pursuing a volume pathway in project grants significantly reduces success in cooperative agreements by 18.7%, suggesting that agencies may interpret this experience as a lack of collaborative capacity. Furthermore, while both pathways in cooperative agreements produce cross-agency learning and reputational spillovers, volume proves especially effective for NPOs with this experience, enhancing access to both awards types by up to 11.8%. Our findings highlight strategic trade-offs in managing government funding. For NPO leaders, the optimal funding strategy depends on existing experience: depth is most effective for organizations with project grant histories, while volume better serves those experienced in cooperative agreements. For federal program officers, funding histories should be interpreted relative to the award being evaluated. Prior cooperative agreement experience signals collaborative readiness in ways that project grant experience does not.
authors: Telesilla Kotsi* (The Ohio State University); Gloria Urrea (University of Colorado Boulder); Sebastian Villa (University of Colorado Boulder)

session_name: Hiring, Skills, and Labor Market Dynamics
title: Skill-Biased or Skill-Agnostic Hiring? Evidence from the U.S. Semiconductor Industry
abstract: Understanding how firms adjust labor demand in response to industrial policy and technological change is essential for assessing large scale domestic manufacturing feasibility. Initiatives such as the CHIPS and Science Act and the Inflation Reduction Act suggest a period of substantial job creation and increased risk of labor displacement. Whether the United States can build sufficient industrial capacity under these conditions depends on how firms respond to market thinness induced skill shortages, and policy induced shocks. In this paper, we examine hiring behavior in the U.S. semiconductor industry following the $50 billion CHIPS and Science Act. We ask whether firms facing expansion adopt skill-agnostic or skill-biased hiring strategies, whether they prioritize or relax specific skill requirements, and the extent these patterns vary across firm types. While existing literature documents that worker transitions are often costly and uneven, it provides limited evidence on how firms adapt skill requirements in practice. We address this gap by comparing the skill profiles of incumbent occupations and of newly hired workers, where new hires are identified using data from Lightcast. We construct a population-weighted skill profile by integrating OEWS and O*NET data, and identify occupation-specific specialized skills relative to the population baseline. Then, we assess whether the skill magnitude of new hires for those specialized skills more closely resembles incumbents, the general population, or falls in between. This framework provides a systematic way to assess whether firm hiring aligns with occupational skill requirements or reflects broader labor market availability.
