session_name: Hiring, Skills, and Labor Market Dynamics
title: Redeployment or Hiring? R&D Characteristics, Organizational Capabilities, and Strategic Human Capital Sourcing in Multi-Business Firms
abstract: Industry shocks reallocate profitability across business units, often forcing multi-business firms to reconfigure their human capital. When a focal business unit experiences a sudden growth inducement, should the firm redeploy employees from other units or hire externally? I develop a task-resource matching view in which sourcing decisions reflect not only transaction and adjustment costs but also the benefits of aligning an employee’s knowledge with task requirements. I study inventor (i.e., engineers and scientists) inflows to ethylene-related business units of petrochemical firms after the U.S. shale revolution, which sharply lowered ethane input costs and increased U.S. ethylene margins beginning in 2011. Using LinkedIn career histories linked to patent records, I observe inventors entering ethylene units of large petrochemical firms (2011-2015) and classify their tasks as downstream new application development or upstream operational efficiency. Consistent with the matching view, firms are more likely to hire externally for new application development roles but rely more on internal redeployment for operational efficiency roles, even after accounting for local hiring frictions and within-firm task relatedness. In addition, these task-contingent patterns are weaker in firms with stronger knowledge recombination capability and more clustered intrafirm inventor networks, suggesting substitution between external hiring and internal knowledge generation/coordination capacities. Additional tests show that external hires bring more novel prior-task knowledge and that performance is highest when the sourcing mode matches task type.
authors: Kyungsoo Kim* (Georgia State University)
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work

session_name: Hiring, Skills, and Labor Market Dynamics
title: Skill-Based Measures of Workforce Readiness Across Canadian Regions
abstract:
Assessing whether regions possess the workforce capabilities needed to support industrial change is a central concern for policymakers, firms, and regional development organizations. Existing research has examined labor mobility, firm behavior, and responses to specific demand shocks, but such approaches are often difficult to use as general, ex ante diagnostics for regional strategy. This paper introduces a capability-based framework for measuring regional workforce readiness using occupational skill proximity.
The method combines occupation-level skill profiles with regional occupational employment data to construct employment-weighted regional skill endowments and assess their alignment with the requirements of a target occupation. The resulting readiness measure captures latent occupational capacity embedded in existing workforce composition rather than predicted transitions, wages, or job creation. Conceptually, the framework treats labor as a stock of capabilities shaped by past economic activity, providing insight into what regions are structurally prepared to support.
Building on prior task and skill-based analyses of labor markets, including recent work in the US context, the approach emphasizes interpretability, transferability, and consistent comparison across places. Applied across Canadian urban regions using harmonized occupational employment and standardized skill information, the framework enables systematic assessment of workforce readiness across cities. An illustrative application shows that readiness changes with the skill threshold used, yielding a broad set of possible occupational options at lower thresholds and a smaller set of closely related occupations that are more realistic candidates for targeted training at higher thresholds.
For policymakers and regional development practitioners, the framework offers a practical tool to align workforce development strategies with realistic, place-based industrial opportunities. More broadly, the paper contributes to industry studies by reframing labor as a stock of capabilities that shapes feasible paths of regional transformation.
authors: Rohan Sharma* (The University of British Columbia); Wouter Bam (The University of British Columbia)
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work

session_name: Hiring, Skills, and Labor Market Dynamics
title: Designing industrial policy to create good jobs in an age of AI: Suggestions from history
abstract:
A “good jobs” or “high road” strategy promotes both equity and efficiency. In this strategy, highly-skilled workers make innovative and sustainable products ; their productivity enables high wages for workers, good products for consumers, and fair profits for managers, while promoting a clean environment.  (See for example books by Paul Osterman; Zeynep Ton; articles by Helper 2009; Luria and Rogers).
Over the past 40 years, there have been a variety of efforts to build on new technologies and managerial practices to achieve  good jobs, including CNC machining; lean production; flexible automation; smart manufacturing, and now AI.  This high road model has long been proposed (including by me), but has only rarely been adopted in the US.  
The difficulty of adoption has been (at least) two-fold: First, the high road (or “ good jobs strategy”  works only if a company adopts several practices at the same time. It must improve communication skills at all levels, create mechanisms for communicating new ideas across a supply chains levels and functions, and provide incentives to use them. Merely getting the prices right (adding taxes or subsidies to correct for market failures) is not sufficient to build these capabilities. Instead, it makes sense to provide technical assistance services to firms directly, and to develop eco-systems of collaborative supplier relations, patient capital  -- not just siloed workforce training efforts. 
Second, many of the benefits of the high-road strategy accrue to workers, suppliers, and communities in the form of higher wages and more stable employment. Profit-maximizing firms do not take these benefits into account when deciding, for example, how much to invest in training. Many firms will provide less than the socially optimal amount of general training because they fear trained employees will be hired away by other firms
 This paper (a draft chapter of a book I’m writing) will explore a variety of examples of efforts to create good jobs. It will draw on a variety of interviews and plant visits I’ve conducted over the past several decades in the industry studies tradition.   Today we again have a new technology in the works, artificial intelligence, that some argue could be used to augment worker capabilities and bring a new era of abundance and prosperity for all.  The paper will draw suggestions from these past technology and management innovations to provide suggestions for managers and public policymakers about how to design strategies that might make this promise more of a reality.
authors: Susan Helper* (15)
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work

title: Emerging Manufacturing Technologies and the Valley of Death: Skilling Innovation Workforce
abstract:
The journey of an emerging manufacturing technology from initial conception to adoption is fraught with multiple challenges. A significant barrier during this complex odyssey is the Valley of Death (VoD) – a metaphorical chasm representing the problems in translating promising research findings into commercially viable products. Literature has recognized the importance of skilled innovation workforce as a catalyst for successful commercialization and a vital bridge across the VoD. Despite a rising interest in the development of innovation workforce, there is a dearth of research scholarship exploring what types and range of skills are needed for a future ready innovation workforce operating in the VoD. The problem becomes more pronounced from the perspective of emerging manufacturing technologies workforce active within the VoD. Hence, the challenges for diffusion and adoption of emerging manufacturing technologies have increased many times.  
Skilling of emerging technologies workforce has been discussed in the relevant streams of literature i.e., innovation systems, emerging technologies, higher education and absorptive capacity. This research through a mixed-methods approach, therefore, investigates the level of engagement among the aforementioned four strands of scholarship. Our hypothesis is that the four domains do not engage with each other, thereby disconnecting important findings for developing skilled innovation workforce for successful management of complex emerging manufacturing technologies through the VoD. Through a bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review we test our hypothesis to identify the level of connection/disconnection between the related strands of literature and propose policy interventions to reduce gaps between research and industry for developing a futuristic skilled innovation workforce for emerging manufacturing technologies. 
The research objectives include: (1) Identifying the critical skills and competencies required for technology transfer and commercialization in the context of emerging manufacturing technologies. (2) Analyzing the role of a skilled innovation workforce in bridging the gap between R&D and market deployment. (3) Developing a conceptual framework that illustrates the relationship between a skilled workforce, technology transfer, absorptive capacity, commercialization, and innovation policy.
authors: Athar Mansoor* (University of Cambridge); Eoin O' Sullivan (University of Cambridge)
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work

title: How U.S. Semiconductor Firms Created an Engineering Labor Shortage and How to Fix It By Bringing Back Workforce Reinvestment
abstract: This research and policy report surveys the research over the last several decades on how the U.S. semiconductor engineering workforce was built up in the 20th century and how it was disinvested in the 21st century. The report additionally analyzed workforce data from the top seven U.S. semiconductor companies (comprising 82% of U.S. semiconductor sales in 2021) and government sources. The report argues that an important under-discussed reason why the industry fell behind in the first place is that American semiconductor companies disinvested in their American workforce by offshoring white-collar jobs, disproportionately laying off Americans, hiring guest workers (including H-1B and Optional Practical Training (OPT) workers, and disinvesting in American engineers and education in the 21st century. Meanwhile, semiconductor companies claimed an engineering labor shortage in the 2000s to advocate for the retention of international students through expanding guest worker programs such as STEM OPT, while pulling back on investing in advanced semiconductor education. Additionally, qualitative interviews with eight current and former American semiconductor engineers supplemented the historical analysis.  The interviews revealed experienced American engineers who were attracted to the industry through employer education incentives, training, and retention programs that produced a stable early to mid-career for them.  Additionally, the government played a key role in providing veterans with the educational opportunity to shift into the industry with the GI Bill. These careers were disrupted because of permanent layoffs firms committed to, along with a shrinking quantity and quality of jobs for industry engineering professionals.  21st-century disinvestment practices diverged from past successful American workforce initiatives that firms undertook, such as raising salaries during engineer shortages and developing retention, recruitment, and education programs. Workforce decisions made by U.S. semiconductor firms were detrimental not just to American professional workers but also to U.S. firms and the United States. The solution for the industry is that the engineering labor market needs to be tightened by reducing the number of white-collar guest work permits in order for semiconductor employers to bring back financial incentives, as they’ve done in the past, to attract American STEM students and workers to the industry. Government policy should safeguard defense and leading-edge semiconductor jobs and prioritize the needs of American workers by reinvigorating the military veteran to semiconductor industry professional pipeline.
authors: Brian Dan-Ding* (Institute for Sound Public Policy/Rutgers University)
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work

title: Assessing Workforce Readiness for Electric Vehicle Battery Manufacturing Plants in the U.S.
abstract: Investment in electric vehicle (EV) and associated battery manufacturing has increased sharply in the past decade, driven by plans for new large-scale gigafactory-sized facilities. Despite the scale of these development plans, the workforce readiness of candidate geographies remains poorly understood. This study estimates the technical labor makeup of large-scale EV battery manufacturing facilities at the occupation level, and assesses extent to which local labor markets in the continental U.S.  are positioned to absorb one of those facilities. We suggest a new method for estimating plant occupational makeups from resume data and advance skills-matching heuristics by using real-world occupational transition data to inform our assumptions Our findings suggest at least two distinct labor models for EV battery manufacturing facilities, one engineering-intensive, and one more labor-intensive. Metropolitan areas, the Rust Belt, and the “Battery Belt” in the Southeast U.S. exhibit a lower level of labor supply strain than the rest of the country, indicating greater potential to fill plant employment locally. Additionally, we identify that industrial engineers are a bottleneck occupation regardless of geography or plant type, and existing announced locations for gigafactories vary substantially in their baseline workforce readiness. Together, these findings highlight the importance of considering labor availability into industrial siting decisions and suggest a role for targeted workforce and industrial policy to improve alignment between manufacturing investments and local labor markets.

title: Ability-centric Worker-Task Assignment Framework in Apparel Manufacturing
abstract:
The transition toward Industry 5.0 calls for human-centric production systems that embrace workforce diversity rather than treating it as variability to be minimized. This shift is increasingly urgent as firms draw on broader labor pools, including people with disabilities, to address labor market challenges. Yet traditional operations management approaches often rely on aggregated worker categorizations, such as disability status or skill levels, that compress multidimensional ability profiles and obscure task-relevant strengths.
This paper introduces an ability-centric framework for worker-task assignment that moves beyond deficit-based perspectives to embrace a strength-based approach. We represent both workers and tasks along the same ability dimensions - workers as vectors of ability levels and tasks as vectors of ability loads that quantify how sensitive processing times are to each ability (i.e., importance of each ability in task performance). This shared representation makes worker-task fit explicit, enabling assignment decisions based on dimensional alignment of abilities on a granular level. 
We examine this framework in collaboration with Peckham, Inc., a vocational rehabilitation organization operating garment production lines where approximately 75% of workers have disabilities. Using a bi-objective optimization model that balances productivity and fairness simultaneously, we trace how these outcomes move together as emphasis on each objective changes. 
Our analysis reveals the following key insights. First, we show that representing tasks and workers at a granular ability level makes worker-task fit visible and actionable. By quantifying abilities of workers and tasks as vectors, the framework provides a foundation to match workers to tasks where they are most likely to succeed based on their specific strengths and the alignment of those strengths to what a task requires. This operationalizes a strength-based approach that echoes Henry Ford’s insight that not all tasks require full physical capacity, and workers with limited abilities can perform well when assigned to tasks that align with their specific ability profile.
Second, through bi-objective optimization, we show a nonlinear efficiency-fairness trade-off relationship. We find that considering fairness in line optimization can improve fairness (i.e., even distribution of workloads across workers) with a modest decrease in productivity. More importantly, as the system places higher emphasis on fairness, it introduces a significant increase in systemic flexibility as a byproduct, measured by the number of workers who can be assigned. The framework leverages task-specific ability requirements to allow the line to integrate diverse ability profiles.
Third, this framework introduces significant opportunities for practice by providing a clear pathway for workforce management, such as targeted training to improve workers’ capability and career advancement that contribute to performance improvement and workplace well-being. Moreover, on a line-level, it enables line managers to identify which specific ability dimension is driving a bottleneck. By pinpointing whether a workstation is slowed by an ability misalignment or an a specific ability’s overload, management can plan targeted augmentations such as assistive technology or task redesign.

title: Embedded Greenhouse Gas Emissions in U.S. Soybean and Soybean Meal Trade and Sustainability Implications for Global Supply Chains
abstract:
Global soybean and soybean meal (SBM) markets play a critical role in food, feed, and bioenergy systems, yet their environmental impacts vary widely across production regions and supply-chain pathways. This study quantified the cradle-to-market greenhouse gas (GHG) emission intensities for U.S. soybean and SBM exports in 2023 using the Food System Supply-Chain Sustainability (FoodS³) model, integrating county-level soybean production and crushing data, land-use change (LUC) and carbon emissions, and international trade flows.
Results showed that U.S. soybean exports had an average cradle-to-market emission intensity of 1.49 kgCO₂e kg⁻¹, while SBM exports averaged 1.12 kgCO₂e kg⁻¹, with production and LUC accounting for more than 80% of total emissions. Transport and processing contributed relatively little compared with upstream production processes. Emission intensities varied by several-fold across export corridors and destination markets, driven primarily by whether sourcing counties reflect long-established cropland or recent agricultural expansion. Because routing through specific ports and soybean crushers aggregates upstream emissions heterogeneity, national averages mask substantial within-country variation that is consequential for buyers, policymakers, and downstream industries.
A case study of SBM-derived crude protein embedded in exported pork diets demonstrated that relative to U.S. pork produced with U.S. SBM, feed-related GHG emissions were approximately 13× higher for Brazil-based pork produced with domestic SBM, 8× higher for China-based pork produced with domestic SBM, and 4× higher for China-based pork produced with imported U.S. SBM. Overall, the analysis highlighted the importance of spatially explicit supply-chain GHG accounting to support climate-aligned trade, procurement, and biofuel expansion policies in global agri-food systems.

title: Supply Chain Interventions by States Promoting the Competitive Viability of their Dairy Producers Facing Federal Regulations that Affect Distribution Costs: The Case of West Virginia
abstract: Federal Milk Marketing Orders (FMMO) regulate the orderly flow of milk from dairy farmers (producers) to market and set milk prices for producers in the United States (U.S.). The 2000 FMMO revisions appear to have mixed effects on U.S. states’ milk production. Some states experienced growth while others, such as West Virginia (WV), experienced contraction. The June 2025 revisions prompted the question, how can states intervene to enhance the competitive viability of their dairy industry? To answer this question we develop a multi-period two-echelon vehicle-routing problem mixed integer linear program (MILP) with inventory. Our MILP exploits network scale economies and transportation density economies to grow WV producers' market extent and leverage the higher prices in the 2025 revisions. We use the MILP as a framework to develop several policy scenario analyses to promote the competitive viability of WV producers. The WV Legislature authorized the West Virginia Department of Agriculture (WVDA) to assist small dairy producers, allowing WVDA to act on our recommendations. We discuss our contributions to (1) the two-echelon VRP literature, (2) theory at the intersection of public policy and supply chain management, and (3) the agricultural economics literature. We present practical implications for policy makers and dairy professionals including limitations of our research, which we hope spurs future research.

title: The Lone Rancher: Digital and AI-Mediated Governance in Upstream Cattle Production
abstract:
How do digital and AI-mediated technologies reshape informal organizing in upstream industry contexts? We examine this question through a qualitative study of the U.S. cattle ranching industry, focusing on how ranchers coordinate land, labor, and animals. Although beef is priced and traded in well-developed markets, upstream activities in cattle ranching have historically been coordinated through informal organizing, including relational ties, local knowledge, and negotiated discretion among ranchers, workers, market intermediaries, and public land managers. Prior technological change in the industry has centered on genetics, animal health, and quality assessment, leaving these informal organizing arrangements largely intact. In contrast, recent advances in GPS-enabled headcollars, drones, and remote monitoring technologies, however, introduce new forms of visibility and control into this land-intensive industry.

Drawing on extensive interview data, including ranch owners, ranch hands, livestock auction operators, agricultural extension officers, veterinarians, and participants with experience interacting with the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), we analyze how digital monitoring technologies reconfigure informal organizing in cattle ranching. Our findings describe a shift from community-based forms of informal organizing, characterized by shared norms, interpersonal trust, and face-to-face coordination, toward more centralized and market-like arrangements in which authority is enacted through data, metrics, and remote oversight. These technologies enable individual ranchers to manage larger herds with fewer workers while reducing reliance on ongoing traditions involving relational coordination with local networks, intermediaries, and land managers. We conceptualize this transformation as a movement from relationally embedded organizing toward data-mediated control, altering how authority is exercised and how coordination is achieved across loosely coupled actors. This shift situates cattle ranching within a digital and AI-mediated era of industry governance and highlights how technological change reshapes informal organizing in settings traditionally governed through social relations.

title: Quantifying Battery Electric Vehicle Affordability in the United States
abstract: Electric vehicle (EV) adoption in the United States remains constrained by affordability barriers, with growth concentrated in higher price segments rather than in affordable vehicle markets. This study presents a novel bottom-up approach to assess EV affordability by combining synthetic household data representing over 150 million U.S. households with machine learning-based expenditure modeling and comprehensive vehicle market data. We constructed household-level financial profiles using Public Use Microdata Samples and trained an XGBoost model on 2019 Consumer Expenditure Survey data (26,000 households) to predict spending-to-income ratios across major categories. Local vehicle markets were defined using 90-minute driving isochrones from census tract centroids, incorporating 19 million vehicle listings from approximately 60,000 dealerships nationwide in 2024. Our analysis reveals that battery electric vehicles (BEVs) are growing fastest in price segments above $40,000, with minimal growth in segments below $30,000. While 99% of Americans have access to at least one internal combustion engine vehicle (ICEV) per person within their budget, only 63% have equivalent access to BEVs—a dramatic improvement from 10% in 2018, but still far from parity with ICEVs. Approximately 25% of Americans have access to fewer than one BEV for every two people. The BEV-to-ICEV ratio within budget averages approximately 1:50 across most of the country. Subsidies have differential impacts across market segments: a $10,000 incentive increases accessible driving range by 22% for new cars, 40% for new SUVs, 39% for used cars, and 27% for used SUVs. This study provides policymakers with granular, location-specific insights for designing targeted incentive programs that address persistent affordability gaps in the transition to electric mobility.

title: Unintended Consequences of Technology Neutrality:  A Comparative Analysis of US and Chinese Industrial Policy in the EV and Battery Sectors
abstract: Recent industrial policies in advanced economies have been increasingly shaped by the climate-security nexus. Geopolitical interests and green industrial policies increase the need for policy alignment, while at the same time, they can increase the risk of contradicting policy targets. In this paper, we seek to analyse the unintended consequences of supply and demand-side industrial policy in the US and Chinese electric vehicle (EV) and battery sectors. The US has largely maintained a technology-agnostic stance when it comes to ‘picking technologies’. Given pre-existing capabilities and established supplier networks, US OEMs naturally chose nickel-based cathodes (NMC or NCA) for early EV models. However, recent geopolitical restrictions have sought to limit the reliance on supply chains with so-called Foreign Entities of Concern (FEOCs), thereby implicitly favouring lithium iron phosphate (LFP). We argue that this has led to unintended consequences where policies effectively favoured battery chemistries where the US does not have capabilities, and without providing specific (LFP) supply side policies.  In contrast, China, through its NEV credit subsidy and the 863 program, took a much more targeted approach by specifying performance metrics such as safety, costs, or manufacturing scale to influence the choice of battery technologies. To compare the two cases, we created a novel database that allows us to map supply and demand-side policies in each country. We conclude that governments should, where appropriate, consider making explicit technology choices, as otherwise the private sector will choose what is readily available or cost-effective, but which might undermine the government’s industrial policy goals.
authors: Keno Haverkamp* (University of Cambridge); Guendalina Anzolin (University of Cambridge); Simon Collinson (Zhejiang University); Xiayu Zhai (Peking University); Eoin O'sullivan (University of Cambridge)

title: Trade Exposure and the Direction of Green Technological Change in the Global Automotive Industry
abstract:
The transition toward electric vehicles (EVs) has proceeded unevenly across automobile-producing countries, even among those with comparable industrial capacity. Existing literature emphasizes domestic policy choices, market size, and infrastructure, but gives less attention to the role of international trade in shaping national innovation trajectories. This paper examines whether—and how—export-market exposure influences the direction and pace of technological change in the automotive sector.
We focus on the political economy of producer–consumer linkages, arguing that exporters are shaped not only by domestic policy incentives but also by regulatory and demand conditions in the markets they serve. Using a panel of major automobile-producing countries over roughly fifteen years, we construct export-weighted measures of exposure to destination markets with differing EV-related regulatory stringency. We pair these measures with country-level indicators of EV-oriented innovation, including patenting activity in electric propulsion and battery technologies, as well as domestic EV adoption outcomes. Exploiting temporal variation in destination-market policy tightening, the analysis shows that greater exposure to stringent regulatory environments is associated with more rapid shifts toward EV-oriented technological development, while exposure to less stringent markets corresponds to more incremental transition paths.
The findings point to a mechanism through which global trade integration conditions green technological change: export-oriented industries adjust their innovation strategies in response to external regulatory and market pressures, with consequences that spill back into domestic production and adoption. More broadly, the paper speaks to debates on industrial policy and international political economy by showing how cross-border economic linkages shape national responses to low-carbon transitions, with implications for the governance and political sustainability of green industrial transformation.
authors: Hengrui Liu* (Tufts University)

title: Responding to Polycrisis: Industrial Relations and Strategic Action in the German automotive industry
abstract:
The German automotive industry is currently facing a profound transformation process. A key challenge is the transition to electromobility, which requires substantial investments in new technologies, batteries, and software. At the same time, demand for electric vehicles and political framework conditions remain uncertain, making planning and profitability difficult. Global competitive pressure has also increased significantly, particularly from Chinese manufacturers, which are technologically advanced in electric vehicles and produce them at low cost. In addition, high production costs in Germany, such as energy prices and labor costs, are weighing on competitiveness. This leads to cost-cutting programs, adjustments in production and job losses. The structural transformation is also reshaping the labor market, as traditional jobs disappear and new skills are required.
In this paper, we explore how the actors within Germany’s system of industrial relations are responding to these challenges, which approaches and strategies they develop, what kinds of labour conflicts arise, and what impact restructuring has on labour regulation. Our analysis is based on case studies of companies in the automotive industry as well as an investigation of industry-level collective bargaining and political lobbying by the collective associations of labour and capital. The core questions we will tackle are: (1) How do works councils react to the polycrisis in their interactions and negotiations with management? (2) What instruments of collective bargaining that cope with these transformations are developed by trade unions and employers’ associations? (3) What demands do the collective actors address to the state and how far do they cooperate in doing this? Based on these questions, we will try to assess the challenges these developments pose for German industrial relations as a whole, given that the automotive industry still forms the backbone of the German model of partnership and corporatism in industrial relations.
The paper is based on findings from the project ‘Digital and Ecological Transformations in the Regulatory Environment of Labour Relations,’ funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG).
authors: Alexander Bendel (University of Duisburg-Essen), Thomas Haipeter (University of Duisburg-Essen)

Hospital Stockpiling Ahead of Shortages: Evidence from the US Opioid Supply Chain
abstract: Drug shortages in the United States remain persistent. When shortages occur, timely and equitable access to the affected drugs and clinical substitutes is essential for patient care. Yet we know little about which hospitals secure supply ahead of and during an imminent shortage. We examine the 2017 nationwide, supply-induced shortage of injectable opioids using multi-echelon transaction data, and ask: (1) how the remaining inventory is distributed once production is disrupted, and (2) how substitutes are accessed in the period surrounding the event. We find uneven allocation and substantial pre-shortage stockpiling of substitutes by a small subset of hospitals, reinforcing “haves vs. have-nots” disparities in pharmaceutical access.

title: Turning a Blind Eye: Role of Pharmacy–Supplier Sourcing Channels in the Opioid Epidemic
abstract: With more than 645,000 deaths since the 1990s, the opioid crisis has been one of the worst health crises in the United States. Previous research has demonstrated that the crisis is primarily initiated and fueled by the oversupply of prescription opioids. This trend has raised significant concerns regarding the effectiveness of government monitoring efforts, which rely on pharmaceutical suppliers to identify and report suspicious pharmacy orders. In response, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) has primarily blamed large national suppliers and increased regulatory pressure on them. In contrast to the DEA's focus on large suppliers, we investigate how pharmacies' use of other sourcing channels contributes to over-dispensing. Using the DEA's ARCOS database and leveraging the 2010 OxyContin reformulation as a quasi-experiment, we analyze more than 350 million opioid transactions between 610 suppliers and 90,920 pharmacies in the US from 2006 to 2014. Our results show that independent pharmacies sourcing a higher share of opioids from small suppliers and chain pharmacies engaging in the self-distribution of drugs through their vertically-integrated supply network exhibit higher levels of over-dispensing. Specifically, independent pharmacies with a 10 percentage point higher share of small suppliers and chain pharmacies with a 10 percentage point higher share of self-distribution in their supply base exhibit 2.6% and 7.2% higher over-dispensing, respectively. We further provide evidence on how the sourcing strategies of pharmacies are associated with higher prescription opioid-related mortality rates at the county level. These findings suggest that focusing regulatory efforts on large national suppliers may overlook the role of supply network characteristics contributing to drug diversion. By highlighting the roles of small suppliers and self-distribution practices, our study underscores the need for a more comprehensive regulatory approach to combat the opioid epidemic effectively.

title: Regulating Powerful Intermediaries: The Impact of Curbing Intermediary Practices on Supply Chain Outcomes
abstract:
Supply Chain Intermediaries (SCIs) account for a significant share of economic activity across many product industries, contributing over one-third of the United States’ gross domestic product (GDP). We observe an increasingly common pattern in which SCIs have gained considerable power, such as traders in agriculture, distributors in alcohol, or GPOs in the healthcare industry, and have adopted practices to extract disproportionate gains in the supply chain. In this paper, we examine how regulating such practices of powerful SCIs affects supply chain outcomes. We focus on retail pharmacy as our context and Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) as SCIs that not only manage pharmacy claims but also, as powerful SCIs, determine which drugs will be covered and how much retailers and manufacturers will be paid, thereby influencing the flow of products, money, and information across the supply chain.
We focus on regulating the ‘Spread Pricing’ practice in which the SCI charges payers (government entities or private employers who pay for products purchased by eligible members or employees as part of a benefit plan) more than it reimburses retailers (from whom the members or employees buy the products) and retains the difference, known as ‘spread,’ an amount determined by and proprietary to the SCI. In our context, Spread Pricing was among the first SCI practices to attract scrutiny, including a payer audit in the Ohio Medicaid program that found a $208M (31.4%) spread charged by SCIs in 2018, which led the payer to ban this practice beginning in 2019. We leverage this exogenous event to investigate whether implementing the ban improved SCI practices and supply chain outcomes. We use secondary data from CMS Medicaid across multiple US states and employ the Synthetic Control Method with Forward Selection Panel Data Approach (fsPDA) to construct a synthetic control unit, Synthetic Ohio, as a weighted average of control states that resemble Ohio but did not experience the policy intervention.
By comparing Ohio with Synthetic Ohio, we found an initial and significant decline in payer expenditures between Q2 2018 (when the audit was conducted) and Q1 2019 (when the ban was enforced). However, we found an overall increase of approximately 15% in payer expenditures post-ban. We further applied a difference-in-differences approach and found that, compared with neighboring states, Ohio's post-ban drug sourcing shifted toward manufacturing facilities outside the United States, which have been associated with lower quality standards. To summarize, the ban on Spread Pricing in Ohio led to an overall increase in payer expenditures and a counterintuitive shift in drug sourcing toward lower-quality drugs. 
Our study has practical implications for regulators and other supply chain members regarding how banning SCI practices may elicit counterresponses from powerful SCIs, thereby contributing to ongoing policy debates in the retail pharmacy industry, particularly as other states consider adopting similar regulations to curb intermediary power. Our research also has broader implications for other industries—such as food, agriculture, alcohol, and healthcare—where powerful SCIs increasingly dominate and where similar regulatory challenges are emerging.

title: Offshore Manufacturing of Innovative Drugs: Evidence from U.S. Pharmaceutical Firms’ Reliance on Specialized Drug Manufacturers
abstract: Pharmaceutical manufacturing often separates drug development from large-scale production through contract development and manufacturing organizations (CDMOs). Over the past two decades, United States pharmaceutical firms have increasingly relied on offshore CDMOs, drawing sustained attention from patients, regulators, and the media due to concerns over drug supply security. We argue that entrepreneurial pharmaceutical firms are more likely than established firms to rely on offshore CDMOs. Entrepreneurial firms typically lack the financial and manufacturing resources needed for in-house production. Although external partnerships can alleviate these constraints, collaborations with established firms expose entrepreneurial firms to heightened risks of knowledge appropriation. Consequently, entrepreneurial firms turn to specialized third-party manufacturers, particularly CDMOs. Because manufacturing experience for pharmaceutical products is unevenly distributed across locations, with a substantial share accumulated by CDMOs located outside the U.S., this reliance often takes the form of offshore contracting rather than partnerships with domestic manufacturers. This reliance intensifies when entrepreneurial firms develop first-mover products. We define first-mover products as first-in-class drugs that introduce a new mechanism of action, thereby giving rise to a new therapeutic class. Developing such drugs requires scaling production processes under heightened regulatory scrutiny and limited prior manufacturing precedent, further increasing reliance on offshore CDMOs. Using a 2025 cross-sectional sample of U.S. pharmaceutical manufacturing contracts, we find results consistent with our arguments. These findings suggest that pharmaceuticals particularly important for patients—those developed by entrepreneurial firms and involving first-in-class drugs—are disproportionately manufactured offshore, revealing a source of vulnerability in the U.S. pharmaceutical supply chain.

title: Type 2 Diabetes Screening under Capacity Constraints: A Health Care Systems Analysis
abstract:
In the United States, type 2 diabetes and prediabetes affect a large and growing share of the adult population, yet a substantial proportion of high-risk individuals remain undiagnosed. In practice, diabetes screening operates not merely as a clinical decision, but as an institutionalized gatekeeping mechanism shaped by clinical guidelines, payment incentives, and care delivery workflows. BMI-based thresholds have become the dominant criterion for determining screening eligibility, embedding a simple and scalable rule into routine practice. However, in a post-pandemic environment characterized by persistent primary care workforce shortages, constrained screening capacity, and increasing heterogeneity in population risk profiles, reliance on legacy screening rules raises important system-level and policy questions.

When screening criteria are institutionalized as gateways to preventive care, their design influences not only clinical efficiency but also the perceived fairness and social legitimacy of health care systems. Persistent misalignment between formal screening thresholds and underlying risk distributions may allow unmet health needs to accumulate outside the system, potentially generating sustained policy pressure on medical and insurance institutions. These concerns are particularly salient for individuals who do not meet conventional obesity criteria but nonetheless face elevated metabolic risk, highlighting the need to reassess how screening opportunities are prioritized under resource constraints.

This study conceptualizes type 2 diabetes screening as a capacity-constrained health care system decision problem rather than solely a predictive task. Using nationally representative survey data from the United States, the analysis compares traditional BMI-based screening rules with an alternative risk-based prioritization approach derived from explainable risk stratification models using non-laboratory variables. Methodologically, the study applies explainable risk-based models to evaluate the system-level performance and missed-case distributions of alternative screening rules under fixed screening capacity constraints. By holding the overall proportion of individuals screened constant, the analysis mirrors real-world limitations faced by health systems and payers, allowing a direct comparison of how different rules allocate limited screening resources across populations.

The study focuses on detection efficiency, patterns of under-detection, and subgroup differences, with particular attention to normal-weight adults and demographic heterogeneity. Rather than presupposing superiority of any single approach, the analysis evaluates whether risk-ranked screening strategies offer potential advantages in aligning screening decisions with population risk under uncertainty.

Overall, this study aims to provide a policy-relevant analytical framework and empirical evidence base to support reassessment and potential updating of U.S. type 2 diabetes screening guidelines. More broadly, it illustrates how screening rule design functions as a system-level policy choice with implications for efficiency, equity, and institutional credibility in capacity-constrained health care systems.

title: Reformulation and Algorithmic Framework for Fractional Queueing-Based Optimization Problems
abstract:
We develop a comprehensive framework for modeling, reformulating, and solving network design queueing-based optimization problems. The network consists of a series of interdependent queueing systems with variable number of servers and endogenous service time and arrival rate, and aims at responding promptly to time-sensitive demand. Defining the number of servers deployed at a facility as a decision variable significantly increases the complexity of the problem formulation. The resulting model is a fractional nonlinear integer problem that includes factorial, polynomial, and exponential terms, as well as summations where the term count is a decision variable. The MILP reformulation framework encompasses five main steps and is general enough to be applied to the main queueing systems, such as M/M/K, M/G/K, G/M/K, and G/G/K. Specifically, we introduce new quasi-multilinearization and multilinearization processes for high-degree polynomials and develop novel analytical methods providing closed-form formulae to calculate the coefficients of multilinear monomials. We devise a branch-and-cut algorithm, solving at each node. an outer approximation of the MILP problem which is gradually tightened through the dynamic introduction of lazy constraints and valid inequalities. 
Notably, we derive a new family of nested valid inequalities and demonstrate their computational effectiveness.  To test our approach, we consider the problem of designing a responsive network for medical emergencies (cardiac arrests, opioid overdoes). The objective is to minimize the average response time to urgent demands and to increase the chance of survival of patients, while deciding the location of facilities, and the deployment and assignment of emergency vehicles. Numerical tests on real data show the applicability of the reformulation and algorithmic framework.
authors: Nguyen Nam* (George Washington University); Miguel Lejeune (George Washington University)
category: Health Care Systems, Biotechnology, and Pharmaceuticals

title: Stochastic Pandemic Mitigation Model: Ensuring ICU Access Without Overburdening Society
abstract: Key objectives for policymakers deciding on pandemic mitigation include safeguarding the healthcare system by ensuring reliable access to ICUs for patients, while simultaneously limiting mitigation measures to avoid overburdening society. These goals are pursued under uncertainty in the illness's transmission rate. We propose a multi-period mixed-integer nonlinear chance-constrained stochastic programming framework that addresses these requirements. We capture the pandemic dynamics through a compartmental epidemic model. We design a solution method that features the (i) deterministic and equivalent reformulation of the nonlinear chance constraint using a Boolean method, (ii) quadratization of the set of nonconvex constraints via linearization techniques for polynomial terms and exponential functions with integer arguments, (iii) construction of the envelope of bilinear terms defined on a specific domain with a non-trivial upper bound on the product of two variables, and (iv) derivation of valid inequalities exploiting the problem's combinatorial structure. The proposed framework generalizes well to alternative mitigation functions and is applicable to nonconvex polynomial chance-constrained problems beyond epidemic mitigation. Our experiments with COVID-19 data confirm the computational efficiency and scalability of our approach, demonstrating that the solutions are stable, reliable and perform well out-of-sample, and robust even under uncertainties in other key model parameters. Our results show that it may be optimal to delay the onset of mitigation and that the optimal strategy can include periods of lenient mitigation in between. This research addresses a gap in the literature on nonconvex polynomial chance-constrained problems and introduces a new second-order cone formulation for the envelope of bilinear terms.
authors: Janne Kettunen* (The George Washington University); Miguel Lejeune (The George Washington University)

title: Response Latency in Asynchronous Care Queues and ED Utilization: LLM-Based Measurement of Patient Message Acuity and Complexity
abstract: Operational delays in decentralized service systems can induce cross-channel substitutions. Digital patient portals provide a novel setting in which delayed response may shift demand toward the emergency department (ED). Studying this mechanism is difficult because structured records do not capture the severity and complexity embedded in patient messages at arrival. We address this measurement problem with an LLM-based pipeline that scores patient-initiated medical advice messages, then combine these text-derived measures with a discrete-time hazard model of downstream ED utilization. Results from 441,806 patient-initiated threads suggest that unanswered messages predict higher short-run ED use, concentrated early in the waiting period. The study shows how AI can recover latent demand signals from unstructured patient text and suggests that some ED demand reflects operational delays among patients who already have outpatient access, not only uninsured access gaps.

title: How Does Generative AI Affect Theories of the Firm?
abstract: Following Coase’s seminal work on the nature of the firm, academic scholars have sought to understand and define a firm, the rationale for its existence, and its boundaries. With the rise of Generative AI, which brings about transformational changes in resources, constraints, means to perform, and strategic orientation, this paper reviews established theories of the firm--Transaction Cost Economics, Agency Theory, Incomplete Contracts Theory, Resource-Based View, and Platform & Ecosystem Theory--to predict  possible effects of AI on the boundaries, internal structure, and overall functioning of a firm. Generative AI offers new capabilities in content generation, pattern recognition, and learning and improving. We characterize these functions as automating, augmenting, autonomous tasking, hyper-personalizing, and virtualizing. We then examine their effects on key parameters that define the nature of the firm, while challenging foundational assumptions such as bounded rationality and opportunism. We argue that generative AI partially restores rational economic agency at both the individual and firm levels, while introducing new forms of opportunistic behavior. In parallel, we assess the extent to which it may reconfigure existing externalities, contractual arrangements, transaction costs, and processes of knowledge formation. Taken together, we identify key forces at play and develop propositions on governance structures, the resources that become more salient, the likely organizational form of a firm, and the emergence of new inter-firm dynamics. We conclude by discussing whether a new theory is needed in light of these advancements.
authors: Boyoon Chang* (Dartmouth College); Geoffrey Parker (Dartmouth College); Marshall Van Alstyne (Boston University)

session_name: Generative AI and the Future of Work
title: Beyond Productivity: Evaluating the Hidden Costs of Generative AI in Software Development
abstract: AI-assisted programming tools are increasingly adopted to enhance developer productivity by automating routine tasks and accelerating software development. While early evidence highlights short-term productivity gains, our study shows that excessive reliance on AI can unintentionally accelerate the accumulation of technical debt, leading to escalating maintenance costs and eventual revenue erosion. Drawing on interviews with software engineers and insights from the literature, we build a dynamic simulation model to examine the long-term impacts of AI-assisted coding under varying conditions of project horizon, legacy-system interaction, developer skill, and market dynamism. Our results reveal that productivity benefits follow an inverted-U pattern: there exists a “sweet spot” where AI assistance improves overall performance, but beyond this threshold, compounded technical debt undermines system maintainability and profitability. We further show that greenfield environments and fast-evolving markets can tolerate higher levels of AI assistance, whereas brownfield (legacy) settings and teams with less skilled developers are substantially more susceptible to long-term decline. We identify technical-debt retirement as a strategic guardrail that can help sustain AI benefits over time. These findings demonstrate that AI-assisted development is not simply a choice of productivity tool, but a strategic decision that must consider programming environment constraints, system longevity, skill composition, and market factors. Finally, we discuss implications for theory and management.

session_name: Generative AI and the Future of Work
title: Synthetic Creativity and Human Talents: How Generative AI Reshapes Value in the Music Industry
abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into creative industries challenges conventional valuations of human capital. This study investigates how the revelation of AI-generated content reshapes perceived value in the music industry. Leveraging the natural experiment of a trending musician’s AI nature revelation, we employ a difference-in-differences strategy to estimate how audience engagement changes once they learn the act is AI-generated. Our results reveal a significant algorithm aversion among audiences, with negative sentiment spilling over to adjacent human musicians. Musicians in genres perceived as low in humanity experience a relative decline in engagement compared to those in high-humanity genres, with those stylistically closer to AI suffering greater losses. Furthermore, musicians with less established career capital are disproportionately affected. Our findings demonstrate AI's context-dependent impact and provide a framework for understanding evolving work and valuation structures in the arts.

title: The Institutional Economics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Higher Education: A Transaction Cost Analysis of University Transformation
abstract:
Why do universities persist in their current bundled form - integrating research, teaching, credentialing, and socialization within hierarchical organizations - when alternative arrangements for knowledge production and transmission have proliferated? This paper applies transaction cost economics (TCE) to answer this question and to analyze how artificial intelligence (AI) may fundamentally transform the institutional logic of higher education. While canonical organization theories describe how universities function internally - as loosely coupled systems (Weick, 1976), legitimacy-seeking entities (Meyer & Rowan, 1977), or organized anarchies (Cohen, March, & Olsen, 1972) - they do not explain why the bundled form emerged and persists. TCE provides this foundation (Coase, 1937; Williamson, 1985), demonstrating that universities internalize functions whose coordination through markets would be prohibitively costly due to verification challenges, monitoring difficulties, appropriability problems (Teece, 1986), and the tacit nature of professional knowledge transfer (Polanyi, 1966).

The paper makes three contributions to organization theory. First, it extends TCE into higher education, developing a systematic account of why credentialing solves signaling problems in labor markets characterized by information asymmetry (Spence, 1973; Akerlof, 1970), why instruction addresses monitoring challenges that market-based provision cannot resolve (Nelson, 1970), why research bundling enables knowledge appropriation under weak intellectual property conditions (Arrow, 1962; Teece, 1986), and why socialization transfers tacit expertise that resists market coordination (Lave & Wenger, 1991). Second, and more fundamentally, the paper advances transaction cost theory by distinguishing between marginal and parametric technological effects on governance structures. Prior technologies - printing, broadcasting, the internet - produced marginal effects: they reduced certain transaction costs while leaving the fundamental parameters that favor bundled governance intact. This explains why universities absorbed these technologies without institutional displacement, and why MOOCs failed to disrupt traditional institutions despite initial predictions (Hoxby, 2014; Reich & Ruipérez-Valiente, 2019). Artificial intelligence differs because it transforms the parameters themselves. AI does not merely make monitoring cheaper; it changes what monitoring means when human and machine contributions become indistinguishable (Cotton, Cotton, & Shipway, 2023). AI does not simply reduce information asymmetry; it creates new forms of asymmetry regarding algorithmic processes while dissolving traditional asymmetries regarding expert knowledge (Agrawal, Gans, & Goldfarb, 2018).

Third, the paper integrates TCE with institutional theory (DiMaggio & Powell, 1983) to explain organizational persistence and change under technological disruption. The analysis yields a typology that maps university functions according to AI substitutability and verification complexity, generating propositions about which institutional arrangements face displacement (content delivery, routine assessment), which gain distinctive importance (professional identity formation, ethical development, research apprenticeship), and which become contested terrain where institutions and markets compete on verification capacity (complex skill development, collaborative capabilities). The framework provides principled criteria for distinguishing between functions that remain essential - continuing to solve transaction cost problems AI does not address - and those that are historically contingent, persisting only through legitimacy and inertia.

For industry studies scholars, this paper demonstrates how transaction cost analysis can illuminate institutional transformation in knowledge-intensive industries facing technological disruption. The distinction between marginal and parametric technological effects has implications far beyond higher education, providing theoretical grounding for understanding why some technologies produce incremental adaptation while others precipitate genuine institutional transformation (Langlois, 2003). For policymakers navigating AI's impact on the higher education industry, the framework offers tools for anticipating which institutional arrangements will prove durable and which require fundamental reconceptualization - a question of considerable consequence as institutions, employers, and governments grapple with AI's implications for workforce development, credentialing, and knowledge production.
authors: Pelin Bicen* (Suffolk University )

title: Leading by example for synergy: The roles of transactional and relational governance on buyer-supplier labor standards alignment
abstract:
Improving labor conditions in supply chains requires the effective alignment of labor standards across upstream and downstream members. Deviant behaviors (e.g., noncompliance of labor codes) by any member can wreck significant reputational and financial damage across the entire chain, even if other members uphold superior labor standards (Hartmann & Moeller, 2014). Therefore, many firms make efforts to not only adopt and implement labor standards within their own firms, but to also “cascade” these standards to their suppliers (Wilhelm et al., 2016). 

Despite the broad literature that examines labor responsibility in supply chains, there exist two important gaps that limit our understanding of its effective implementation across supply chain actors. First, most of this research has focused on the labor performance of individual firms (i.e., buyer or supplier), while overlooking potential alignment in labor standards between the two parties. This alignment is critical as labor responsibility requires the ongoing collaboration of both buyer and supplier. Second, there is a need to better understand how buying firms can achieve a certain consistency and quality of labor standards across supply chain tiers. Studies have long debated over the merits of transactional and relational governance, with many advocating for the complementarity of both approaches (e.g., Alghababsheh & Gallear, 2021; Locke et al., 2007). However, much of this debate remains in theoretical argument with a paucity of empirical evidence—largely due to the lack of data on labor standards in buyer-supplier dyads. 

In this study, we draw from research on buyer-supplier dependence and embeddedness to explore the alignment in labor standards between suppliers and their major customers. Using 474 unique supplier-major customer dyads over 14 years (2010-2024; collected from the Compustat and Sustainalytics databases), we performed hierarchical analysis to estimate the direct and interaction effects of customers’ labor standards, transactional governance, and relationship history on their suppliers’ implementation of labor standards.

Our findings show that a supplier’s labor standards is significantly influenced by that of its major customer. In addition, a longer relationship history between the customer and supplier, but not the use of transactional mechanisms, is associated with greater supplier labor standards (LS) implementation. The synergistic effects of the two governance mechanisms however, depend on the customer’s own labor standards: transactional and relational mechanisms work in complementary ways only when the customer itself demonstrates high levels of LS implementation; when customer implementation levels are low, the use of neither mechanism is effective in influencing suppliers’ labor compliance, thus unveiling the intricacy of their complementarity. These results depart from the traditional view of the buying firm as an enforcer of labor-related expectations and suggests that there should be more emphasis on the exemplary role of the buying firm in leading labor compliance. To our knowledge, our study is the first to provide large-scale quantitative evidence on the likelihood of alignment between buyer and supplier labor practices, and the governance mechanisms that influence this alignment.
authors: Yinyin Cao* (University of Michigan - Dearborn); Yoon Hee Kim (Kennesaw State University)

title: Playing Fair? Environmental Impacts and Practices of Facilities in Minority Communities
abstract:
We investigate facility-level heterogeneity in environmental impacts and impact reductions in host communities. In doing so, we address an important research gap at the interface between Environmental Justice (EJ) and Operations Management by advancing the emphasis on EJ from an aggregative geographic level to the facility level, where managerial decisions are made. Specifically, we examine how similar facilities operating in minority and non-minority communities differ in the generation, mitigation, and avoidance of environmental impacts, and we explore operational, organizational, and institutional drivers of these differences. We draw on chemical release and environmental risk data from the US EPA’s Toxics Release Inventory and Risk-Screening Environmental Indicators Model, demographic data from the US Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, and additional facility-level data from the National Establishment Time Series. Using matching and panel data methods, we find robust evidence that facilities in minority communities generate greater environmental impacts. However, we do not observe significantly higher levels of impact avoidance or mitigation compared to facilities in non-minority communities. While seemingly encouraging, such an approach is deficient from an EJ standpoint due to the persistence of contemporaneous disparities. Our additional analyses reveal that the disparities are driven by facility age, operational complexity, leanness, chemical usage, process controls, and regulatory frameworks.
We provide actionable insights for managers and regulators. Managers can enhance EJ outcomes through the following actions that address the underlying drivers of greater environmental impacts in minority communities: retiring or refurbishing ageing facilities, rationalizing or substituting particularly hazardous process inputs, investing in leaner operations, and enhancing process controls. We identify high-disparity sectors for prioritizing regulatory efforts and recommend the consideration of cumulative local environmental burdens in policy design and enforcement.

title: Effect of Voluntary Climate Targets on Corporate Decarbonization
abstract:
Several firms across various industries have announced voluntary climate targets: in 2021 Apple committed to reducing its combined scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions 62% by 2030 using 2019 as the baseline year, whereas Walmart committed in 2020 to reducing its scope 1 and 2 emissions 65% by 2030 against a 2015 baseline year, with an interim reduction target of 35% by 2025. AstraZeneca committed in 2021 to reducing scope 1 and 2 emissions 98% by 2026 against a 2015 baseline year, and to reducing scope 3 emissions 90% by 2045 against a 2019 baseline, along with several interim targets. These targets vary in terms of their ambitiousness (e.g., 50% vs. 100% reduction), coverage (e.g., scope 1 only vs. scopes 1 and 2), and time horizon (e.g., 5 vs. 30 years). Moreover, a firm can periodically revise its targets over time as governance or market factors influence the firm’s confidence in reaching its targets. In this paper, our goal is to understand how such differences in decisions related to voluntary climate targets influence corporate decarbonization. By characterizing the factors that drive target-setting decisions and progress related to corporate decarbonization paths, we aim to contribute insights that can help with both a) monitoring our collective progress towards a net-zero future and b) designing mechanisms that align firm incentives with societal goals.

Corporate decarbonization has recently received some attention in the literature. For example, Bolton and Kacperczyk (2025) find that firms that announce targets subsequently experience greater reduction in their scope 1 emissions, with more aggressive targets and those focused on absolute emissions exhibiting greater effectiveness in driving decarbonization. However, this analysis is limited to the impact of targets on scope 1 emissions only, without focusing on the dynamics of target-setting (e.g., updates over time). There is also mixed evidence regarding whether or not financial instruments, such as carbon offsets, meaningfully contribute to achieving decarbonization goals (see, e.g., Stolz and Probst 2025). To our knowledge, no research has yet explored the dynamics of corporate target-setting from a firm-level perspective. We contribute to the literature by focusing specifically on how firm-level target trajectories influence a firm's decarbonization decisions across all three scopes.

To answer our research question, we use data from CDP, formerly known as Carbon Disclosure Project, which houses the world’s largest primary corporate environmental dataset. We have CDP emissions data for over 20,000 firms across the world between 2010 and 2024, which we cross-validate with company reports and databases tracking emissions as well as announcements of climate targets.

Companies draw on operational (e.g., changes to product/process design), financial (e.g., purchase of offsets), and supply relationship (e.g., supplier selection and requirements) levers to meet their decarbonization commitments. We examine the dynamics of the decision process firms face at different points in the target lifecycle. By identifying the causal relationship between targets and decarbonization outcomes, this work will provide guidance for corporations as they design their decarbonization goals, and for policymakers and environmental groups seeking to guide corporate engagement in climate action.

title: ESG Challenges in Large-scale Infrastructure Projects
abstract:
Large-scale infrastructure projects are critical for economic development and societal well-being, with global spending on infrastructure accounting for more than 10% of the world GDP. These projects are unique in nature in terms of design and location, technically complicated and large in scale, and thus have great level of impact on various stakeholders. While these projects are notorious for their frequent cost overruns and delays, the large physical nature makes such projects especially susceptible to various sustainability challenges.

While various factors have been studied extensively as drivers of project performance, sustainability challenges, specifically, the role of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) risks remains largely underexplored in operations management literature. This study investigates ESG risks in large-scale infrastructure projects by examining ESG-related challenges and risks over the life cycle of projects.

We analyze 280 large-scale infrastructure projects from the World Bank, spanning transportation, water, and energy sectors across 64 countries. We first develop a comprehensive project-related ESG taxonomy through text analysis using text data obtained from ESG-related documents and project documents from the World Bank. Using the identified ESG terms, we measure intensity of ESG-related risks at the point of project planning and after completion of the projects. By comparing project appraisal documents with completion reports, we identify which ESG risks are likely to be anticipated during planning versus those that emerge over the project's implementation and examine how these emergent challenges influence project performance outcomes.

This study contributes to operations management by investigating an underexplored intersection of infrastructure project management and sustainability and showing ESG-related factors as important drivers of project performance.

session_name: Green Innovation and Sustainable Energy Strategies
title: Harnessing the Wind: Temporal Conditions of Plural Sourcing Strategies  in the Electric Utility Industry
abstract:
Work has examined the make-versus-buy decision mainly by conceptualizing it as a binary choice, contrasting internal production with external procurement. A growing body of scholarship is investigating plural sourcing, an alternative arrangement in which firms simultaneously engage in internal production and external procurement (Parmigiani 2007, Puranam et al. 2013). Firms employ plural sourcing for a variety of reasons including minimizing transaction costs (Puranam et al. 2013), reducing risk and opportunism (Hefetz et al. 2014), mitigating the challenge of ambiguity and information asymmetry (Heide 2003, Sorensen et al. 2023), facilitating knowledge spillovers (Potter and Paulraj 2021) and integrating external knowledge (Parmigiani and Mitchell 2009, Krzeminska et al. 2013). Taken together, plural sourcing acts as a distinct sourcing mode that offers benefits not attainable through exclusive reliance on internal production or external procurement. 
In practice, firms adjust their sourcing strategies over time. However, plural sourcing literature generally takes a rather static view, treating a firm's simultaneous use of multiple governance modes as a fixed state. As a result, the dynamic nature of sourcing strategies and the temporal sequencing of governance decisions has been largely overlooked. Work shows that past contractual relationships or in-house production shape, often constraining, future sourcing decisions (Argyres and Liebeskind 1999, 2002; Cohen and Levinthal 1990, King and Tucci 2002, Leiblein and Miller 2003). As such, earlier decisions tend to reinforce existing governance structures, resulting in firm-specific, path dependent patterns of governance. Although governance inseparability helps explain the persistence of particular governance modes, it does not account for why firms employ combinations of governance modes for similar transactions over time. To address this gap, we incorporate the temporality of sourcing decisions. Specifically, we ask: Under what conditions do firms transition from a single governance mode to plural sourcing, and what mechanisms drive these transitions? 
We examine the sequencing of governance arrangements in sourcing a single input, focusing on firms’ initial sourcing decisions and subsequent adjustments. We compiled a database of U.S. electric utilities sourcing wind energy from 2005-2015. We examining utilities that had not previously engaged in wind power generation to identify the factors driving their initial sourcing choices. Next, we turn to utilities that have completed their initial wind procurement and explore the conditions under which they continue to rely exclusively on a single sourcing strategy or transition to a plural sourcing approach. 
Our analysis corroborates findings that utilities are more likely to procure wind energy when they face heightened pressure from policy mandates (Fabrizio 2013, Fremeth and Shaver 2014, Dutt and Cunningham 2025) and social activists (Sine and Lee 2009, Delmas and Montes-Sancho 2010). We also find that prior sourcing experience reinforces governance choices in subsequent transactions (Fabrizio 2012, Kim 2013). More importantly, by comparing the determinants of wind sourcing decisions across the first- and second-stage analyses, we find that the factors driving initial wind sourcing decisions differ systematically from those shaping subsequent governance choices. Whereas initial sourcing is largely influenced by external pressures and constraints, the transition from exclusive external procurement toward plural sourcing is driven primarily by a utility’s internal asset configuration. In the absence of such enabling conditions, utilities tend to remain on established governance paths or defer further action, thereby reinforcing path dependence. When these enabling conditions are present, however, firms are more likely to depart from prior governance trajectories and adopt plural sourcing arrangements. Our findings demonstrate that the determinants of internal production and external procurement are not necessarily symmetrical. This asymmetry underscores the importance of analyzing governance modes on their own terms and provides new insights into why firms adopt plural sourcing strategies.
authors: Jennifer Woolley* (Santa Clara University); Shaohua Lu (Santa Clara University)

session_name: Green Innovation and Sustainable Energy Strategies
title: Co-creation over R&D: External Knowledge as the Engine of Green Innovation in Italian SMEs
abstract:
Firms are increasingly expected to pursue green innovation while operating under conditions of economic, regulatory, and technological uncertainty. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), these pressures are particularly acute due to limited internal resources and constrained R&D capacity. This paper examines how SMEs adapt to these conditions by relying on external knowledge and co-creation rather than internal R&D as the primary engine of green innovation. 
Using survey data from 6,646 Italian firms, we analyze how collaboration with demand- and supply-side actors, digital technologies, and government support shape firms’ engagement in green innovation and subsequent performance outcomes. We employ a two-stage structural equation model to examine both the determinants of green innovation and its economic effects.
The results show that co-creation with customers, suppliers, and formal partners is a strong and consistent driver of green innovation across SMEs. Digital technologies, such as IoT and big data analytics, further enable firms to absorb and integrate external knowledge, while public policy instruments positively support green innovation adoption. In contrast, internal R&D intensity has no direct effect on green innovation for most SMEs, highlighting a shift toward network-based and collaborative innovation models. We find limited indirect effects of R&D through co-creation, primarily among medium-sized firms. Importantly, green innovation is associated with higher productivity and revenue growth, indicating that environmentally oriented innovation can strengthen firm performance even under uncertainty. Overall, the findings suggest that co-creation and policy-supported digital capabilities play a critical role in shaping sustainable industry dynamics, particularly for SMEs navigating uncertain economic and regulatory environments.
