title: Implementing a Comprehensive Intervention to Promote Sustainable Agricultural Practices in India
abstract:
Rice residue burning (RRB) is a major challenge in northwest India due to unsustainable agricultural activities and is a major source of hazardous air pollution. Despite the availability of sustainable agricultural practices (SAP), their adoption remains limited because existing implementation efforts are often fragmented and poorly coordinated, preventing farmers from using these practices effectively in the presence of capacity and behavioral constraints. This study examines how a well coordinated and comprehensive intervention can overcome these implementation challenges and allow large-scale adoption of SAP.    

We study a community-level intervention implemented in 82 villages in Punjab, India. The intervention was implemented through an integrated delivery system that aligned key stakeholders, ensured timely access to resources, and integrated engagement within local communities. Using satellite-based fire detection data from NASA and demographic data from the Indian Census, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences design to evaluate the environmental outcome. We also analyze data from a primary survey to assess economic outcomes. Our results show that the intervention reduced the RRB incidents by 26% in the treated villages compared to the control villages. In addition, farmers who adopted SAP experienced a 2% increase in wheat yield (wheat succeeds rice in the cropping cycle). A complementary cost-effectiveness analysis indicates that the coordinated intervention achieves better implementation results at relatively modest incremental fiscal cost. 

This study demonstrates that SAP become effective only when integrated within coordinated delivery systems that build physical and organizational capacity and leverage local social norms. For policymakers and program managers, the findings highlight the importance of investing in implementation infrastructure, stakeholder alignment, and community-level engagement rather than relying on standalone incentives or regulations. For practitioners, the intervention provides a scalable framework for implementing integrated programs that simultaneously improve environmental performance, farm productivity, and operational reliability in resource-constrained agricultural value chains.
authors: Subhankar Saha* (Ahmedabad University); Haritha  Saranga (Indian Institute of Management, Bangalore); Sriram Narayanan (Michigan State University); Chandrakant Pradhan (Confederation of Indian Industry)

title: Coordinating Market Actors for the Public Good: Competition Policy as the Industrial Policy of Democratic Economic Governance
abstract:
We start with the premise that industrial policy refers to the mechanisms that governments use to shape markets in the pursuit of a specific outcome, and that these policies are critical to governments' ability to initiate and guide change in the economy. Building on this premise, our paper analyzes the ways that industrial policy strategies can be undermined by market actors’ attempts to unfairly capture or distort markets, and discusses how competition laws, institutions, and policy frameworks have been used in the U.S. to strengthen democratic economic governance, and thereby enable other industrial policy successes. 

Our overarching argument is that democratic economic governance should be an explicit goal of governments’ industrial policy strategies given that it is a prerequisite for achieving other industrial policy priorities, and that competition policies are critical to achieving this goal. 

We start by looking directly industrial policies intended to achieve the goals most often associated with competition policy: addressing the consequences of monopolization and unfair market practices. In these cases, competition policy is clearly the preferred form of industrial policy mechanism, but we also review how other industrial policy tactics can be used to achieve similar outcomes.

Second, we discuss industrial strategies intended to prevent incumbent firms from becoming barriers to change—such as when they restrict innovation, block the entry of new businesses, or otherwise slow the development of new industries. Practices like killer acquisitions, refusals to deal, or exclusive dealing arrangements can undercut new competitors—and sit squarely within the regulatory mandate of antitrust laws.

Third, we look at policy strategies for preventing the incumbents of one industry from leveraging their market power to capture the gains of new or adjacent industries that are the target of governments’ industrial policy campaigns. Here, we discuss the use of industry-specific safeguards, common carriage obligations, and guardrails against financial sector capture.

Fourth, we review strategies for ensuring that the beneficiaries of industrial policies do not themselves use public support to unfairly capture the gains of their own industries, or establish themselves as the barriers to future change. We discuss the importance of integrating competition policy mechanisms into industrial strategies from the onset, and of structuring industrial policies to distribute public support fairly to all market actors in a given sector.

Finally, we look at international markets where, we argue, the monopolistic actors are countries rather than companies. We look at the supply chain risks of geographically concentrated production, and the geopolitical risks of countries weaponizing chokepoints. Here, countries’ classic industrial strategies for building up new industries mirror competition policy strategies for strengthening competitors to monopolist firms. 

This paper was published in the May 2025 issue of the Competition Policy International Antitrust Chronicle, but has not yet been presented at a conference. The authors are building on these ideas in their current research and policy advocacy, and so welcome the opportunity to share our thinking with, and receive input and feedback from the ISA community.
authors: Audrey Stienon* (Open Markets Institute)

title: Regulatory Reform and Market Evolution in the Spectrum Commons
abstract: How does a decline in regulatory frictions shape innovation and competition in technology markets—and who benefits most from such reforms? This study examines the Federal Communications Commission’s transformation of wireless device regulation between 1997 and 2001, which reduced certification delays, delegated compliance testing to private bodies, and expanded access to unlicensed spectrum. Using administrative records covering nearly 200,000 equipment authorization applications from 1990 to 2015, we analyze how reductions in procedural costs affected product introduction, firm entry and survival patterns, and competitive dynamics. We document a distinctive pattern of market evolution. Following the reforms, regulatory processing times fell sharply, coinciding with a sustained expansion in product introduction and firm participation, particularly in unlicensed spectrum applications. This expansion was driven disproportionately by new entrants, who accounted for most growth in product variety and experimentation across emerging categories. At the same time, established firms retained survival advantages and remained dominant in technically complex product categories. The coexistence of widespread entrant-led experimentation and incumbent persistence is difficult to reconcile with strong forms of regulatory capture, which would predict disproportionate gains for established firms. Taken together, the findings identify a hybrid competitive regime in which regulatory reform broadens access and experimentation without eliminating capability-based advantages. These results inform contemporary debates on privatized certification, commons governance, and the design of regulatory institutions for emerging technologies.
authors: Haiyang Zhang* (Harvard Business School); Shane Greenstein (Harvard Business School); Roberto Fontana (University of Pavia); Do Yoon Kim (Boston College)

title: Dynamic Competition in Networked Markets: Evidence from US Broadband
abstract: This paper examines how regulatory policies can promote sustainable entry in US broadband. I develop a dynamic spatial competition model that endogenizes market structure, product differentiation, and capacity investment. On the demand side, households differ in internet preferences by demographics; on the supply side, firms set prices and speeds in a static game subject to capacity constraints, and make dynamic expansion and upgrade decisions. To solve the firm's high-dimensional optimization problem, I develop a reinforcement learning algorithm that decomposes decisions across locations while preserving network-wide strategic coordination. In counterfactual analysis, I study two proposed policy interventions: municipal fiber provision and unbundling schemes where incumbents lease infrastructure access. Municipal broadband expands fiber access by 10% but ultimately reduces total welfare by triggering disinvestment from private competitors. This causes outsized harm to lower income households. Unbundling policies generate more favorable outcomes, particularly for price-sensitive consumers. Under a two-part tariff calibrated to the UK's cost-depreciation-based implementation, consumer surplus increases 12% at the expense of incumbents. I find that when one accounts for firms’ dynamic responses, slashing connection fees while increasing usage fees by half can deliver Pareto improvements and an 18% increase in total surplus.
authors: Jennifer Zou* (Harvard University)

title: Who Really Knows How Many Workers and Firms Are in An Industry?
abstract: Federal economic statistics by NAICS code are a key input of numerous scholarly studies of individual industries. These data are generated through two registers of the nation's business establishments, each classified by a NAICS code. One register is maintained by the Census Bureau and one by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Unfortunately, federal law prevents these two registers from being synchronized; as a result, the Census Bureau's count of establishments and employees in one NAICS code can vary substantially from the BLS count for the same industry. This disparity can raise questions about the solidity of a substantial proportion of scholarly industry studies. This paper describes the extent of and reasons for such disparities, recent efforts to reduce or eliminate these disparities, and policy options to do so going forward.

session_name: A Practitioner Panel on Nonprofit Operations Under Funding Uncertainty
title: A Practitioner Panel on Nonprofit Operations Under Funding Uncertainty
abstract: Nonprofits face strategic challenges distinct from those in the for-profit sector, despite deep interdependencies with corporations: they gave over $44 billion to nonprofits in 2024 alone, partner with them in underserved markets, and depend on nonprofit infrastructure (such as food banks and childcare programs) to support the communities where they operate. A central difficulty is the decoupled stakeholder problem: donors fund operations but do not consume services, while beneficiaries receive services but exercise limited influence over organizational priorities, weakening the feedback mechanisms that typically hold organizations accountable and complicating resource allocation during crises. The 2025 funding crisis offers a window into these dynamics, as domestic programs for food assistance and early childhood education experienced significant cuts, the primary U.S. agency for international humanitarian aid was dismantled in weeks, and nonprofits that had built decades of capacity around government funding must now adapt, merge, or close. This panel examines how nonprofits are responding by bringing together leaders from three organizations, including one of the nation's largest food banks, a regional childcare network with national policy reach, and an international medical relief organization operating in over 70 countries, each navigating the same exogenous shock under different operational constraints. Discussion is organized around four themes: how donor restrictions affect operational performance; the gap between measurable outputs and what communities actually need; resource allocation decisions when crisis strikes without time for planning; and the tension between pooling resources with organizations that are simultaneously competitors for limited funding.

title: Lunch & Business Meeting
How Coopetition Dynamics Change as Industries Mature: Evidence from the U.S. Craft Brewing Industry
abstract: We explore how coopetitive preferences change as an industry matures by examining both the macro trends around within-industry collaboration formation and the micro behaviors of partner selection across multiple dimensions of strategic similarity in the U.S. craft brewing industry. Abductively studying multi-brewery collaboration beers from 2007 to 2023,  we find that the rate of coopetition formation increases even as the industry matures. The nature of partner selection, however, fundamentally shifts in two theoretically important ways. First, firms prefer to buffer increasing competitive pressures by dramatically reducing partner similarity on one dimension while maximizing it on another, presumably to improve value creation opportunities. This highlights the strategic importance of multi-attribute trade-off management. Second, high-status incumbents abandon the collectivist "rising tide" logics in favor of self-preservation, clustering with highly similar local peers to pull up the ladder behind them in ways that reduce entry and accelerate competitor exits.

title: Agglomeration Economy Dynamics and Demand Spillovers:  Restaurant Week Effect on Participants’ Neighbors
abstract: Agglomeration economies generate benefits for agglomerated firms. How benefits propagate through an agglomeration is unclear because agglomerations are composed of multiple firms and each firm engages in various activities that might have spillover implications for neighbors. To observe this propagation and identify underlying mechanisms, we leverage some firms taking a specific strategic action that generates benefits for themselves that might spill over to neighbors. Focusing on demand-side (vs. supply-side) agglomeration benefits, we expect that neighbors will benefit more when geographically closer to the action-taking firms (due to lower customer search costs) or when selling similar goods to the action-taking firms (due to what customers the strategic action attracts), but benefit less when both geographically closer and selling similar goods (due to localized competition). Using a quasi-natural experiment featuring establishment-level micro-geographic data of restaurants participating in “Restaurant Week” in Washington DC (an event to stimulate demand), we find that Restaurant Week participants’ neighbors experience heightened demand for several weeks after Restaurant Week. Consistent with our expectations: neighbors benefit more when geographically closer or if selling similar goods to Restaurant Week participants. But the benefit for neighbors selling similar goods is delayed a couple weeks, which is consistent with localized competition initially offsetting spillover benefits. Our results demonstrate how firms taking specific strategic action can lead to spillovers propagating throughout an agglomeration, and how overlapping mechanisms determine who benefits and how much.
authors: Roxanne Jaffe* (Vanderbilt University)

title: The Buc-ee’s Effect: Measuring the impact of shopping tourism on local economies
abstract: The Buc-ee’s gas station and convenience store chain has recently undertaken a campaign of expansion outside of its home state of Texas. As it opens new locations, some observers have suggested the potential for a unique “Buc-ee’s effect” on local economies due to the company’s dedicated customer base. This paper studies point-of-interest visitation data to measure local effects from the opening of Buc-ee’s branch stores from 2019-2025.
authors: Christopher Smith* (University of Southern Mississippi)

title: Optimizing Vessel Transit Efficiency in the Welland Canal: A Simulation-Based Approach to Lock Congestion
abstract: This research investigates maritime congestion patterns within the Welland Canal, a critical artery of the St. Lawrence Seaway transporting over 40 million tons of cargo annually comprising of essential commodities, including grain, iron ore, and manufacturing materials. While the canal utilizes a system of eight locks, the configuration of single (one-way) locks creates significant bottlenecks compared to the twinned (two-way) sections. Utilizing a discrete-event simulation model, this study evaluates vessel speed optimization strategies—specifically when ships should accelerate or decelerate—to minimize transit delays. Furthermore, the research explores operational flexibility within the twinned locks, assessing the impact of unidirectional 'double-flow' scheduling to alleviate peak congestion. The results of this research have the potential to improve the flow of vessels and cargo through the Welland Canal lock system as well as reduce the idling and concomitant fuel consumption associated with vessels queueing to enter the canal.
authors: Ashesh Sinha (West Virginia University); John Saldanha* (West Virginia University)

title: Does Branding Affect Perceived Drug Safety?
abstract: We examine whether brand equity shapes perceptions of drug safety. Using FDA adverse event data, we find that after Pfizer’s COVID-19 vaccine success, reports of side effects for its drugs sizably fell, suggesting the firm’s enhanced brand favorably influenced public perceptions of its drug safety.

title: Data Privacy Regulation and Innovation
abstract: We investigate how data privacy regulations shape research and development. While such regulations aim to increase stakeholder privacy and data security, they can also introduce costs in settings where collecting, analyzing, and sharing sensitive data is central to innovation. We examine this tension in the context of the pharmaceutical industry and the European Union's (EU) General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the most comprehensive data privacy regulation to date. Leveraging firm-level variation in exposure to the GDPR, we find that the regulation lowers clinical trials by 18 percent. Firms also shift the types of projects they pursue: trials are less likely to include sites in the EU, be conducted across multiple countries, and target a narrower set of diseases. Research collaborations decline overall and shift away from new partners towards established relationships. When looking at project outcomes, we observe that trials take longer to complete, are less likely to succeed, and report results with greater delay. The decline in clinical trial activity is greatest among young firms. These findings reveal how data privacy regulations shape not only the rate of innovation, but also the process by which it is pursued and its outcomes.

title: Life cycle assessment of risk‑stratified breast cancer screening: a pathway‑based systems analysis
abstract: The healthcare sector is a significant contributor to greenhouse-gas (GHG) emissions, with radiology-intensive oncology services accounting for a substantial and growing share due to high energy demand, resource-intensive equipment, and medical-waste generation. Among oncology services, breast cancer screening and diagnostic care represents one of the most radiology-dependent clinical pathways in routine healthcare, yet the environmental impacts of this coordinated sequence of services have not been comprehensively assessed from a life-cycle perspective. Existing life-cycle assessments (LCAs) of breast cancer screening have largely focused on individual imaging modalities or isolated procedures, failing to capture the conditional, sequential, and organizational nature of real-world screening–diagnostic workflows and their dependence on patient-specific risk stratification decisions. In this study, we conduct a pathway-based life-cycle assessment of hypothetical risk-stratified pathways informed by current research for breast cancer screening and diagnostic care. The sequence of screening, recall, diagnostic imaging, biopsy, and pathology procedures is modelled for patients stratified into clinically defined low-, average-, elevated-, and high-risk groups, each associated with different expected volumes and intensities of imaging and diagnostic procedures. The results show that risk-stratified screening pathways are associated with an approximately 30% reduction in GHG emissions compared with conventional population-based screening models. Emissions are primarily driven by routine screening and downstream diagnostic procedures, highlighting the environmental benefits of risk-based screening strategies. Methodologically, this study advances healthcare LCA by shifting the analytical focus from individual technologies to entire clinical care pathways, and demonstrates how integrating clinically defined risk stratification can reorganize service delivery to reduce environmental impacts while maintaining clinical validity.

title: Appointment Reliability in Primary Care: Evidence from Adults With ADHD in Epic Scheduling Data
abstract: Missed outpatient primary care appointments reduce access and disrupt clinic schedules, yet the drivers of cancellations and no shows remain incompletely understood in large health systems. This study examines whether adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) exhibit different appointment completion patterns than adults without ADHD in internal medicine and family medicine clinics and quantifies the implications for appointment reliability. Using Epic scheduling data, we construct an appointment level panel including all scheduled primary care appointments during calendar year 2024, regardless of final status (completed, canceled, or no show). ADHD status is defined at the patient level using diagnosis history recorded anywhere in the health system, reducing misclassification that can occur when ADHD is identified only from visit level coding. The primary outcomes are cancellation probability, no show probability, and timing of cancellations relative to the scheduled appointment time. Secondary outcomes include rescheduling frequency and time to next completed primary care visit following a missed appointment. We estimate adjusted differences between ADHD and non ADHD patients using regression models with clinic and provider fixed effects and controls for demographics, payer class, and comorbidity indicators. To strengthen causal interpretation, we exploit within clinic variation over time and conduct sensitivity analyses using alternative ADHD definitions, including problem list based identification and medication evidence. The study contributes to operations management research by providing a scalable measurement approach for appointment reliability using electronic health record scheduling traces and by clarifying whether a clinically identifiable patient segment is associated with systematically different patterns of cancellations and no shows. Findings can inform targeted scheduling and outreach strategies aimed at improving access and continuity in primary care.

title: AI Adoption and Firm Performance: Size-Dependent Effects and the Moderating Role of Regional Innovation Ecosystems
abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) adoption shapes firm performance by combining a large panel of Italian firms observed from 2015 to 2024 with detailed regional indicators of innovation ecosystems. The analysis shows that AI adoption is positively associated with firm growth, both in value added and total factor productivity (TFP). However, the benefits are not evenly distributed across firms. A clear U-shaped pattern emerges: small and large firms achieve the largest performance gains, whereas medium-sized firms benefit less. The regional context further conditions these effects. Firms located in less-developed regions—with weaker innovation infrastructure, lower knowledge creation, and fewer collaboration networks—experience larger performance improvements from adopting AI, suggesting that advanced technologies can substitute for missing external capabilities. Taken together, the results highlight that both organizational scale and regional environments shape the effectiveness of AI deployment. They also indicate that, under the right conditions, AI can support economic convergence by helping lagging firms and regions catch up.

title: From Tolerance to Termination: How Venture Capitalists Decide on Startups’ Invention Failures
abstract:
Venture capitalists (VCs) routinely face the challenge of deciding whether to persist in or terminate investments as new information about startup performance unfolds. In innovation-driven contexts, this decision is particularly complex because technological experimentation inevitably generates invention failures that are ambiguous in their implications—startups’ invention failure can either serve as a signal of learning or a trigger of abandonment. Little is known about when and why failure sustains versus undermines investor commitment. We address this puzzle by conceptualizing VC follow-on investment decisions as an optimal stopping problem in which investors balance the informational value of waiting against the costs of continued commitment.
We develop a formal model in which VCs observe new information about startups’ invention activities and follow threshold-based rules governing investment continuation and termination. The model predicts a non-monotonic relationship between invention failure and investment termination: moderate failure enhances learning and increases the value of waiting, whereas very low or excessive failure reduces expected future payoffs and accelerates exit. Importantly, the model also predicts systematic heterogeneity in stopping thresholds across investors, shaped by differences in experiential depth and breadth.
We test these predictions using a novel dataset that links U.S. venture capital investments to detailed patent application outcomes. Analyzing 16,013 funding rounds involving 2,328 VCs and 3,392 startups from 2002 to 2022, we find robust evidence of a U-shaped relationship between startups’ invention failure rates and the likelihood of VC investment termination. Consistent with optimal stopping logic, termination likelihood is lowest at intermediate levels of failure. Moreover, this relationship varies systematically with investor experience. VCs with deeper technological or industrial familiarity exhibit greater tolerance for invention failure, shifting termination thresholds rightward, whereas VCs with broader experience across technologies or industries terminate investments at lower levels of failure due to higher opportunity costs.
These findings contribute to research on entrepreneurial experimentation, venture capital decision-making, and strategic persistence by offering a dynamic, forward-looking explanation for failure tolerance. By framing investment continuation and exit as optimal timing decisions, this study reconciles competing views of failure and highlights how investor experience conditions the strategic meaning of negative innovation signals. Practically, the results underscore that effective governance of entrepreneurial experimentation depends not only on observing failure, but on interpreting its magnitude and timing relative to investors’ capabilities and opportunity sets.
authors: Shu Deng* (University of Mississippi); Jung H. Kwon (University of Denver)

title: The Value of Cross-Product and Cross-Location Information in Demand Forecasting
abstract: (a) Purpose of the study/piece: Accurate demand forecasting is fundamental to achieving reliable and efficient operations in supply chains, yet forecasting performance remains limited in many real-world environments characterized by high uncertainty, demand variability, and sparse historical data. Traditional forecasting approaches primarily rely on a product’s own historical demand, which restricts their ability to capture market dynamics shaped by substitution behavior, complementary consumption, and competitive interactions across stores. This research examines whether incorporating cross-product and cross-location information can improve item-level forecasting accuracy and identifies the conditions under which such information provides the greatest value.  (b) Research method: We use a transformer-based time-series framework to incorporate these relational features into the analysis. Product-level substitution and complementary relationships are quantified based on historical co-movement in demand, and cross-location information is represented using demand signals from nearby stores identified by geographic proximity. These relational inputs are compared against baseline models that rely only on an item’s historical demand to assess whether they improve forecasting performance and under what conditions the improvements are most substantial. The analysis uses real-world transactional data from a healthcare services company, including more than 90 million observations across over 2,500 locations and 7,000 products. (c) Findings or Predicted Findings: Preliminary results show that incorporating cross-product and cross-location information yields meaningful improvements in item-level forecasting accuracy compared to models that rely only on each item’s historical demand. At this stage, we have demonstrated the proof-of-concept and will continue to fine-tune the analysis. The next phase of the analysis will examine the contribution of different relationship types individually and use post-hoc analysis to see which relationships contribute more to accuracy improvement. We will then compare forecasting accuracy improvements across different demand environments and relationship configurations, enabling clearer interpretation of when and why relational information is most beneficial. (d) This work shows how research can integrate managerial thinking into algorithm development by embedding real operational relationships directly into the modeling process. The research contributes theoretically by demonstrating that relational information across products and nearby stores holds predictive value and improves forecasting performance compared to treating items independently. From a managerial perspective, more accurate forecasts can support better inventory positioning, reduced stockouts, fewer emergency reallocations, and more responsive replenishment strategies. Additionally, the research helps improve understanding of the root reasons behind customer decision-making behavior by revealing how purchasing patterns reflect underlying relational demand dynamics.
authors: Rang* (Rae) Gong (The Ohio State University); Walter Zinn (The Ohio State University); Xiang (Sean) Wan (The Ohio State University); Keely Croxton (The Ohio State University)

title: Stars vs. Centrality: What Matters in New Digital Product Development Teams?
abstract:
We examine how team composition mechanisms, specifically the presence of stars (i.e., high performers) and centrally connected members, shape performance outcomes in new digital product development. Using the video game industry as an innovative setting, we test whether stars are essential for success or whether team members with central connections can provide comparable benefits and substitute for stars.

We assemble a dataset of video game development projects and map collaboration ties from industry credits to construct measures of stardom and network position (including PageRank centrality). We link these team characteristics to new product sales and estimate their effects using causal inference techniques, confirming results across specifications.

Our findings reveal that while stars enhance performance, their presence is not essential in this industry. Instead, centrally connected individuals diminish the impact of stars, illustrating a substitutive relationship between stardom and centrality. Well-connected members act as a human platform that aggregates ties, facilitates information sharing, and connects teams to the larger developer ecosystem, helping firms manage risk and uncertainty in hit-driven markets.

These results contribute to research on innovation and new digital product development by clarifying when network position matters more than star power in assembling product teams. They also offer practical guidance for resourcing and staffing decisions: firms should consider the substitutive relationship between centrality and stardom when making recruitment strategies, team design decisions, and resource allocation for product development. Hiring someone with strong connections can deliver similar results, often at lower cost.
authors: Karthik Ramachandran* (Georgia Institute of Technology)

title: Apparel Closed-Loop Supply Chains
abstract:
The traditional method of apparel production relies on virgin natural (e.g., cotton) and synthetic (e.g., polyester) materials. The manufacturing process follows a mostly linear path: involving fiber extraction, fabric production, dyeing, cutting, sewing, packaging, and distribution. A large majority of apparel consumption occurs in the end-consumer market. Consumer behavior is also largely linear: consumers buy, use, and dispose of apparel at the end of its useful life. The rise of fast fashion in recent years has increased the number of apparel items consumers purchase and the speed at which they are discarded. This linear production-consumption approach places strain on the resources required to produce apparel and requires efficient management of discarded items. Brands (i.e., apparel manufacturers) are increasingly adopting recycled fibers in the production processes.   

The transition from virgin to recycled fibers in apparel production requires fundamental changes in how brands organize their operations and supply chains. We collaborate with a large global apparel brand to understand the tradeoffs and pressure points in the transition. We show that, to transition from a linear to a closed-loop model, brands must adapt their procurement, product design, production, and marketing strategies. We discuss the internal and external challenges brands face in setting up economically and technically viable recycling operations. We also discuss the drivers that can enable the implementation of a closed-loop model for brands, including: i) technical improvements; ii) trade-related policy and legislative incentives and initiatives; and iii) industry-wide collaboration.

title: From sustainability pursuit to place-based outcomes: Urgency and infrastructure in U.S. data center expansion
abstract: This paper examines how place-based infrastructure shapes the translation of corporate sustainability efforts into environmental outcomes under conditions of urgency. Sustainability research often emphasizes the role of sustained effort in improving outcomes, while research on organizations and place highlights how localized infrastructure shapes economic activity. We integrate these perspectives to theorize how urgency makes place-based infrastructure a binding constraint on environmental outcomes despite sustained sustainability pursuits. Using an abductive, pattern-then-probe approach, we develop a mechanism in which environmental outcomes are produced through operational execution tightly coupled to local infrastructure. When urgency accelerates execution beyond the pace of infrastructure adjustment, firms execute through existing systems, whose place-specific characteristics shape environmental outcomes. Empirically, we study the U.S. data center industry and leverage the public release of ChatGPT as a shock that increased urgency for firms developing and deploying proprietary AI models (“hyperscalers”). We compare these firms to colocation providers that lease computing capacity without proprietary models and face more modular demand. We show that urgency does not alter internal facility configuration (e.g., scale or density), isolating facility siting as the primary mechanism. Data centers most exposed to urgency (i.e., large-scale facilities operated by model-developing firms) are disproportionately sited in grid systems with greater power availability and higher fossil fuel dependence, even as firms continue large-scale renewable energy procurement. By separating sustainability intent, pursuit, execution, and outcomes, our findings contribute to the understanding of how urgency reshapes the relationship between sustainability efforts and place-based environmental exposure in infrastructure-dependent innovation.
authors: Angela Ryu* (University of Southern California); Shon Hiatt (University of Southern California)

title: Imported solar photovoltaics contributed to health and climate benefits in the United States
abstract: Global supply chains have played a central role in driving down solar photovoltaic (PV) costs and accelerating deployment globally, but their broader societal benefits are underexplored. Here we quantify the climate, air quality, and health impacts of imported solar panels in the United States between 2014 and 2022. We find that 1 kW of imported solar capacity yields an average of $180 in annualized climate and health benefits, offsetting nearly half the PV module cost in 2020. This imported capacity displaced fossil generation by 305 TWh, avoided 178 million tons of CO2, and prevented an estimated 595 premature deaths between 2014 and 2022. While these advantages are unevenly distributed across regions and demographic groups, residents in non-importing states also benefited from them. These findings provide critical evidence for policy debates on clean energy trade, showing that imported solar capacity delivers substantial public health and climate gains beyond direct cost savings.
authors: Minghao Qiu (Stony Brook University); Gang He* (CUNY-Baruch College); Peter Marcotullio (CUNY Hunter College)

title: Technology Makers as De Facto Job Designers in American Healthcare
abstract: As the U.S. healthcare system hobbles along, key stakeholders look to technology—these days, artificial intelligence (AI)—to improve sectoral performance. But this performance panacea won't come to fruition if it worsens the psychological strain on clinicians by intensifying their workload and narrowing their discretion. Our analysis shows this is precisely what's occurring. Using qualitative analysis of marketing materials from 100 U.S. healthcare AI technology "makers", i.e., developers, marketers, etc., complemented by 19 trade journal articles quoting hospital administrators, we show how makers act as de facto job designers. Makers converge on four value constellations: efficiency, spreadability, and precision—that translate into design imperatives and, in turn, into three solution archetypes: turnkey, configurable, and customizable. Each archetype implies a distinctive job-design bundle. Turnkey systems elevate demands and limit resources; configurable systems provide bounded flexibility with contingent effects; and customizable systems expand discretion, learning, and feedback. We document a market-level "job-design tilt": makers focus on turnkey offerings, where procurement incentives reward rapid, standardized deployment while externalizing adaptation costs to clinicians. The study extends work-design and sociotechnical theory by locating job design in upstream productization and not only in organizational implementation. It also reframes debates on workplace automation by linking market incentives to patterned consequences for work. We conclude with implications for procurement, regulation, and participatory co-design.

title: From Rhythms to Stop, Drop, and Roll: Unpacking the Impact of Algorithmic Management on Discretion in Hotel Housekeeping Work
abstract: A key concern regarding the spread of algorithmic management (AM) beyond gig work is how it reshapes workers' discretion, or latitude to make decisions. When overlaid onto pre-existing routines, AM introduces temporal volatility by dynamically sequencing tasks, allocating assignments, and adjusting pacing in real time. How do such transformations affect workers' discretion over rhythms of work, and how do they respond? Drawing on a qualitative study of hotel housekeeping, the authors show that guest room attendants exercise meaningful discretion over their work, relying on contextualized and embodied knowledge to sequence rooms, adjust pacing, and manage physical effort. AM disrupts these practices by curtailing sequencing and creating pressure, through interruptions, while cleaning rooms. Yet workers actively rebuild temporal structures through "rhythmic reconstitution," blending algorithmic directives with situated knowledge, improvisation, and negotiation. We further evaluate these qualitative findings using an original, recently completed national survey of guest room attendants. Together, the findings reveal how AM transforms discretion over rhythms, advancing studies of technology, the labor process, and temporality in organizations.

title: 'Two Snakes with One Head:' How Automation Creates Relational Cleavages between Interdependent Work Groups
abstract: Even the most advanced technologies typically automate only portions of a work process, rather than the process in its entirety. This "modularization" creates divisions between workers directly affected by automation and those who share the same workspace but perform jobs that have not been so transformed, potentially altering relationships between these two groups. Through a comparative analysis of six e-commerce fulfillment centers, we examine the extent to which partial automation creates tensions between interdependent work groups. We compare functionally equivalent jobs across facilities that use one of three main technologies to complete the same work process: collaborative robots, conveyors, or hand-pulled carts. With field observations and more than 100 interviews, we show that the partial automation that results when robotics are introduced to only select roles creates "automation cleavages"—fault lines between groups that work with the robots and those that do not. Four dimensions of negative differentiation emerge at these boundaries: robotics workers are perceived by their coworkers in other roles as unreliable (blamed for technology malfunctions), unavailable (physically isolated and socially inaccessible), unalike (having different workplace values and levels of organizational commitment), and unworthy (performing easier work requiring less effort). These divisions undermine collaboration and coordination, resulting in slower production, extended downtimes, and decreased workforce satisfaction. The findings challenge optimistic predictions about collaborative robots improving job quality. Instead, partial automation erects social barriers between workers of similar status, producing relational inequalities between automation "haves" and "have-nots" within shared workspaces. Our study contributes to understanding how intelligent technologies transform workplace social relations, extending the work design literature and highlighting the unintended organizational consequences of technological modularization.

title: Contested Automation: Double Indeterminacies, Job Quality, and Union Resistance in Call Centers
abstract: This article analyzes how unions resist the harmful effects of automating technologies on working conditions. Drawing on semi-structured interviews, workshops, and survey data gathered from Canadian and U.S. call centers, it examines union contestation over the effects of self-service "job-replacing" technologies, e.g., self-order forms, chatbots, and interactive voice recognition systems. Building on Smith's conceptualization of "double indeterminacies" within the labor process, we argue that work effort and mobility represent two main domains of contestation over the deployment of automating technologies. The findings show how automation threatens working conditions across both indeterminacies. On the one hand, automation increases work effort by creating errors that must be handled by agents and by subordinating workers to mandated protocols. On the other hand, automation weakens workers' mobility power and job security by making them more replaceable, as it takes over customer inquiries. In response to these changes, unions' collective bargaining provisions for job security protect workers from layoff threats due to automation, while disciplinary and monitoring provisions reduce work intensity arising from work process disruptions. The current article makes two significant contributions. First, we extend the concept of double indeterminacies to understand the impact of emerging automation technologies. By extending this framework, we add greater theoretical precision to analyses of how technologies shape work across two domains. Second, we show how unions' collective bargaining comes into play in the "social shaping of technologies." Specifically, the article highlights that the institutional legacy of past struggles remains effective in protecting workers from harms associated with new technologies.

title: Preannounced Regulatory Inspections: FDA Oversight and Drug Quality Risk
abstract:
When inspecting a U.S. drug manufacturing facility, FDA inspectors arrive unannounced. However, in foreign countries
such as India, FDA inspectors provide significant advanced notice of their inspection, often many weeks or even months
before arriving. We examine the impact of these differing FDA inspection approaches on inspection outcomes and drug
quality. We first use 15 years of data from unannounced U.S. and preannounced Indian FDA inspections at over 200
facilities. Using a matching analysis to mimic the FDA’s model for selecting facilities for inspection, the 15-year dataset
indicates no significant difference in the odds of unannounced U.S. and preannounced Indian facilities receiving the most
severe inspection outcome, implying relatively equivalent drug manufacturing quality. Next, we examine previously unexplored data from two unannounced inspection pilots conducted by the FDA in India. These pilots enable us to disentangle
whether the equivalent inspection outcome result is indicative of similar drug quality or a greater difficulty of detecting
drug quality issues with preannounced inspections. We find that the odds of a facility receiving the most severe inspection
outcome are over 250% higher for unannounced inspections compared to preannounced inspections at the same facility in
India. Finally, using a matched sample of facilities producing over 3,000 drugs, we demonstrate potential consequences of
preannouncing inspections in India, showing that the number of serious adverse events for drugs made in Indian facilities
that experience preannounced inspections are significantly greater than for drugs made in matched facilities in the U.S.
that experience unannounced inspections. Our findings provide the first quantitative empirical evidence that preannouncing FDA inspections may allow drug manufacturers to operate with greater and undetected quality risk.

title: Assessing the Security and Quality of the U.S. Military Health System Pharmaceutical Supply Chain: A Pilot Study (PhaSQ)
abstract:
Abstract: The Nation and military readiness are impacted by the quality, safety, and availability of pharmaceutical products. The Assessing the Security and Quality of the U.S. Military Health System Pharmaceutical Supply Chain (PhaSQ) pilot study benefits the entire Nation by identifying and potentially mitigating the negative impacts of ineffective, impure, or unavailable pharmaceuticals. A lack of resilience and lack of transparency regarding quality in the supply chain, and the reliance on other countries to manufacture crucial drugs, are known national security risks. This project will be completed via four lines of effort. The first line of effort compares the essential medicines lists between the US Department of War (DoW), Food and Drug Administration, Department of Health and Human Services, and World Health Organization. The second line of effort synthesizes recommendations made to the DoW by other government agencies to strengthen its pharmaceutical supply chain. The third line of effort assesses the acceptability of a proposed “red, yellow, green” scoring tool for drug quality, which will include participants from the DoW, other federal agencies, and members from the private sector of the US healthcare system. The last line of effort, undertaken in partnership with Valisure, LLC, evaluates 42 drug products for quality and safety. To date we have completed the first two of our four lines of effort. All lines of effort are expected to be completed in 2026. Findings from this study are anticipated to inform decision making regarding sourcing and distribution of high-quality essential drug products.

title: Assessing the Acceptability of a Proposed Generic Pharmaceutical Quality Scoring Tool for Application in the United States and Military Health Systems
abstract:
Abstract:
Introduction: The Department of War (DoW) commissioned a study to assess the quality and safety of pharmaceutical products critical to the operational needs of the Military Health System (MHS) and develop, apply, and test a quality scoring tool. In this study we aim to assess the acceptability, validity, and utility of a proposed quality scoring tool that incorporates various chemical analysis data.

Materials and Methods: The current study is a qualitative key informant interview study to assess the acceptability of the proposed scoring tool. We recruited participants who are key stakeholders involved in the DoW or US pharmaceutical supply chain, using purposive and snowball sampling. We provide participants with contextual information about the tool in advance of the virtual interview. Two interviewers are present for each interview; one leads the discussion with a pilot-tested interview guide, and the other interviewers record detailed notes. Thematic  analysis of responses will be conducted using NVivo.

Results: At present, we have conducted 16 out of an expected 30 interviews. Participants have provided insights into aspects of the proposed tool and the potential applicability of the tool within the DoW and US health system. We anticipate results from this study will inform policy making regarding sourcing and distribution of high-quality drug products for both the MHS and the Nation.

Conclusions: This is the first study to evaluate the acceptability of a generic pharmaceutical quality tool. We anticipate to complete all analysis and interpretation of results by May 2026.

title: The Foreign Inspection Gap: FDA GMP Oversight of U.S. Drug Imports, 2014–2024
abstract: From 2014 to 2024, U.S. drug imports rose sharply while FDA foreign GMP inspections fell. Analyzing FDA inspection records against import volumes, we found that for every additional billion dollars of drug imports between 2014 and 2019, 23 fewer inspections occurred. Inspection intensity in China dropped from 101.8 to 18.3 inspections per billion USD over the decade. Foreign facility outcome rates with observations ran 1.3 to 1.8 times higher than the U.S. baseline of 49.3 percent, with China at 69.0 percent and India at 62.3 percent. Disparities between MRA and non-MRA countries persisted across the period. These findings provide empirical support for the FDA's May 6, 2025, shift to unannounced foreign inspections and highlight the need for oversight metrics that scale with the globalization of pharmaceutical manufacturing.

title: Grid and electricity demand from AI data centers
abstract: US electricity demand is growing for the first time in decades, thanks in large part to demand for AI infrastructure. The electricity system is having difficulty meeting this demand, which has become a bottleneck for the AI buildout. This session will explore the complex, high-pressure interaction among AI model builders, data center developers, utilities, alternative power providers, and all levels of government, which will determine how AI will be powered in the U.S. The outcome has substantial implications for the economy, national security, and the environment. This panel will provide complementary perspectives from the AI and electricity sectors as well as a critical analysis of the policy issues that must be resolved.

title: National Security Impacts of Pharmaceutical Supply Chain Resiliency in the United States and Military Health System
abstract: Over the past few decades, production of most of America's generic drugs and the ingredients needed to make them has moved to India and China, where regulation is increasingly difficult. Growing concerns over drug quality and safety are evidenced by rampant drug shortages, approximately 76% of which stem from manufacturer quality problems, roughly three drug recalls per day in the United States often related to dangerous impurities, and a growing number of reports of patient harm. A lack of supply chain resilience and transparency, combined with dependence on foreign sources for crucial drug ingredients, poses significant risks to national security for both the general public and the Military Health System. This panel begins with an overview of the Domestic Production of Pharmaceutical Products for the Military Health System project currently underway at the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, after which academic and research partners will discuss the public health and national security consequences of drug shortages through moderator questions covering quality and supply chain resilience, pharmaceutical make-buy-invest strategies, the impact of Drug Enforcement Agency policies on Schedule II controlled substances, Department of War essential medicines and supply chain reprioritization, a framework for supply chain strengthening, and end-to-end supply chain mapping. Audience questions will follow.

title: Break
Timing University Entry: Institutional Pressures and Semiconductor Research Adoption
abstract:
Universities have become central players in regional innovation ecosystems, extending beyond traditional education and research roles to actively engage with emerging technology fields. As universities navigate this expanded mission, they face critical strategic decisions about when and how to enter new research domains, shaped by institutional pressures and peer behavior. This study addresses two research questions: First, when and where did U.S. universities enter semiconductor research, and how did entry patterns evolve? Second, do universities enter in response to peer institutions' entry, and are peer effects stronger for geographically proximate and higher-status peers?
First, we explore the temporal evolution of university entry into semiconductor research, examining temporal distribution distinguishing early versus late entrants, geographic distribution of engaged universities, and clustering patterns. We construct a novel dataset linking Scopus publication data and USPTO patent data. By matching inventor names on patents to university author names, we comprehensively track university engagement in semiconductor research. Second, we investigate university entry strategies through mimetic pressures based on institutional theory, capturing these pressures through peer universities' publication activity and comparing effects from national versus in-state peers, and examining how peer status shapes influence.
This research makes three contributions: First, we examine semiconductor research from the university perspective rather than the traditional firm-centric view. Second, we apply institutional theory to explain university strategic behavior in emerging technology fields, providing a new lens for understanding university research strategies. Third, we demonstrate a methodological approach integrating patent and publication data for comprehensive tracking of university engagement.
authors: Shuqi Sun* (Arizona State University); Maryann Feldman (Arizona State University)

title: Seeding Translational Research: Evidence from Corporate Scientist Migration to Academia
abstract: Why are scientific discoveries with academic origins harder to commercialize than those from corporate labs? We hypothesize that universities prioritize the pursuit of codified scientific knowledge at the expense of practical techniques required to exploit natural phenomena in a scalable fashion. In Joel Mokyr's terms, "prescriptive" knowledge in academia is a secondary concern to the mission of accumulating "propositional" knowledge. We test our theory by showing how a group of corporate scientists migrating into U.S. universities facilitated the commercialization of extant academic research. Using the career histories of 691 former corporate scientists moving to universities on LinkedIn from 2000-2022, we identify 1,280 faculty that coauthor with such "corporate migrants" after their arrival. To isolate the effect of "prescriptive" corporate knowledge, we focus on academics' papers written prior to the migrant's arrival and use Coarsened Exact Matching to identify "control" papers close by with similar commercial potential and within the same field. Difference-in-differences estimates suggest that papers "shocked" by corporate migrants receive 115% more citations by patents compared to control papers (relative to the sample mean). Unobserved scientific quality differences do not seem to drive this result as no comparable effect is found for placebo papers exposed to migrants from other universities. We also find that the added patent citations are not more likely to come from migrants’ former employers, ruling out the possibility that the effect merely reflects redirected corporate attention. Rather, the effect is driven by academic papers shocked by migrants with prior knowledge in high-value scientific instruments, suggesting that the transfer of corporate "prescriptive" knowledge aids with commercializing hitherto impractical academic knowledge. Together, our results suggest that academic research is a poor substitute for "prescriptive" knowledge nurtured at corporate laboratories.
authors: Jungkyu Suh* (New York University)

title: Coopetition in Charging Infrastructure
abstract: The rapid growth of the Electric Vehicle (EV) market is fundamentally constrained by a fragmented charging infrastructure, characterized by the coexistence of multiple proprietary standards (e.g., NACS, CCS). This fragmentation creates consumer range anxiety, complicates strategic investments for automakers, and hinders mass EV adoption. Our research investigates the strategic decision of open-access standardization, where an innovator (e.g., Tesla) allows an imitator (e.g., Ford) to utilize its proprietary charging network: a form of coopetition driven by the innovator’s potential for data monetization. We develop an analytical model that integrates the operational decisions of physical infrastructure investment with the strategic opportunity of monetizing vehicle usage data. Our analysis characterizes the equilibrium investment and access strategies for both firms. We establish that open access is a contingent equilibrium strategy that can generate win-win outcomes for both firms only when the innovator’s data monetization potential is sufficiently high and the imitator’s independent infrastructure is relatively inefficient. Counter-intuitively, we find that the prospect of open access can reduce the innovator’s incentive to expand its physical network, as the core strategic value shifts from physical scale to the depth of collected data. Finally, our social welfare analysis reveals that consumer surplus and total welfare are maximized only under conditions of mutual investment and open access (coopetition), as this configuration simultaneously improves network coverage, alleviates congestion, and ensures interoperability. This study provides critical operational and strategic insights for automakers on optimal network design and standardization, and for policymakers seeking to maximize EV adoption through infrastructure mandates.
authors: Sanchari Guha Niyogi (Institute of Management and Technology, Hyderabad); Prasenjit Mandal (Neoma Business School); Abhishek Roy* (Temple University); Abhishek Chakraborty (Xlri Jamshedpur)

title: The Power and Pitfalls of Techno-Industrial Policy: Evidence from China
abstract: I study how industrial policy shapes innovation by examining China's Strategic and Emerging Industries (SEI) initiative (2010-2018), a large-scale fiscal intervention targeting frontier technology sectors. Employing a staggered difference-in-differences design with city-industry-level patent data, I uncover three key findings: (1) While patent quantity surged by 184%, quality metrics showed minimal improvement; (2) The quantity gains came at a 14% decrease in patent output from untreated sectors, revealing sectoral displacement instead of crowd-in effects; (3) Cities that adopted path-dependent targeting (selecting sectors with pre-existing innovation advantages) achieved over twice the patent growth rates of their counterparts, though without corresponding quality gains. These findings reveal a paradox in China's development model: while achieving unprecedented success in scaling innovation quantity, the nation has yet to realize comparable quality gains - a critical gap as it transitions from 'made' to 'created in China'.
authors: Hannah Wei* (IMF)

title: Reach Out and Heal a Heart: Tele-ICU and Low Virtualization Care Processes
abstract:
Telehealth offers significant potential to improve healthcare delivery, but its benefits are context-driven. It shows clear advantages in consumer-facing, high-virtualization settings and uncertain impacts in high-stakes, tightly coupled processes like Intensive Care Unit (ICU) care. Prior IS research has examined high-virtualization telehealth, such as mental
health. In these settings, patients are active agents, and self-efficacy drives outcomes. Far less attention was given in the ICU context, where continuous monitoring, rapid decision-making, and coordination are critical.
In this paper, we examine tele-ICU, a telehealth technology designed to support ICU care. We use acute myocardial infarction (AMI) as a context to study a low-virtualizable care process. The AMI care process mostly begins with ICUs and requires rapid monitoring, coordination, and reliance on specialized staff. AMI care contributes significantly to hospital readmissions, targeted under the Medicare Hospital Readmission Reduction Program, underscoring their importance. The shortage of cardiac care staff has increased interest in tele-ICU, which can extend expertise across hospitals. However, the comprehensive role of intensivists in the ICU may also affect the impact of tele-ICUs. These countervailing forces motivate our investigation.
Drawing on process virtualization theory and the sociotechnical systems perspective, we develop hypotheses about the direct and interaction effects of tele-ICU, health information interchange, and closed-model cardiac intensivist use on AMI outcomes. Using panel data and a control function approach, we find no direct effects of tele-ICU. We find strong
complementarity between tele-ICU and health information interchange, and separately, between tele-ICU and intensivist staffing. Effects vary by organizational level—hospital, joint-venture, or system—highlighting ICU coordination challenges. 
Our study contributes theoretically by extending process virtualization theory with a sociotechnical perspective to low-virtualization care processes. It helps guide hospital administrators on when tele-ICU can improve the ICU care process. It contributes policy-wise by informing telehealth investment, integration, and post-pandemic efforts to enhance complex care.
authors: Deepika Gopukumar* (Saint Louis University ); Nirup Menon (George Mason University); Sidhartha Das (George Mason University); Amitava Dutta (George Mason University)

title: Path Nets in Pharmaceutical Innovation: A Temporal Dynamics View of Supply Chains
abstract:
Although supply chains are conventionally modelled as networks of firms and flows, this representation obscures the temporal dynamics through which supply chains unfold.
 
Path nets offer a complementary perspective by treating paths, defined as coherent progressions of activity, and their intersections as the fundamental units of analysis. This path–event ontology shifts attention from static structures to the temporal ‘fabric’ of supply chains, making visible the mechanisms that shape flow: coherence, recurrence, interdependence, and inclusion–exclusion.
 
Using a 10-year dataset involving novel pharmaceutical innovations (supported by c. £100M of private and public R&D funding) and over 100 stakeholders collaborating in pre-competitive consortia, we represent the transition from batch-oriented pharmaceutical R&D to continuous and data-driven operating models, not as a linear chain of R&D, regulatory, and manufacturing stages, but as an interwoven set of paths consisting of digital technologies offering new degrees of freedom in terms of novel platforms and equipment, new skills/training and organizational capabilities, and emerging design rules and standards.
 
As efforts were adopted within and across three specialized networks (product, production, and supply chain), we explore how the paths of various technologies and organizations join/separate over the 10 years to create different opportunities for innovation and technological readiness. To do so, we operationalize path nets as temporal hypergraphs, which provide a way to weave multiple, concurrent paths into a temporal fabric (aka, a path net).
 
Three path net categories are observed spanning different TRL ambitions over the 10  years: those that support product-centric innovation, those that support supply chain-centric innovation, and those that support platform approaches that are more multi-disciplinary in nature. We also observed a network survival dynamic where networks became resource-seeking to sustain themselves, including positive flywheel effects.
 
This path net perspective reveals how firm networks manage turbulence under technological, regulatory, and market uncertainty, and how resilience emerges when recurrent paths create coherence, i.e., why some supply chain fabrics of innovation hold together while others unravel.
authors: Tomas Harrington* (University of East Anglia (Uea)); Jagjit Singh Srai (University of Cambridge); Brian Pentland (Michigan State University); Sriram Narayanan (Michigan State University); Nitin Joglekar (Villanova University)

title: Workload Intensity and Task Switching: Managing Workplace Safety through Continuous Monitoring
abstract: We study how work pace, operationalized through workload intensity and workers’ task switching across vehicles, affects workplace safety. Using a unique proprietary industrial data that links vehicle telematics to shift logs, we ask: (i) How does workload intensity affect the rate of safety accidents? (ii) Does task switching condition this relationship? Our results show that higher workload intensity increases the safety accident rate. This effect is amplified when workers frequently switch between tasks and vehicles. To address endogeneity concerns, we employ a two-stage least squares approach using lagged workload as instrument, complemented by a control function approach to account for any residual endogeneity in shift-level workload assignment. Moreover, we uncover a nonlinear workload-safety relationship that identifies a critical workload. Accident risk rises only gradually at low workload levels but accelerates sharply once workload surpasses a threshold. Our post-hoc analysis further reveals important staffing-related insights. Specifically, we find that assigning a quality control/inspection or maintenance/technical support worker to the same shift as the vehicle operator significantly reduces safety accidents. In contrast, adding supervisory or administrative staff yields no comparable safety improvements. This pattern is consistent with supervisors’ limited on-floor presence and highlights the value of on-the-ground technical expertise for detecting equipment and process hazards as they emerge. Overall, we show that workplace safety depends not only on workload levels but also on how work is sequenced and staffed. Safety can be improved by limiting excessive task switching, ensuring on-the-ground technical capacity, and adapting staffing in light of the critical workload intensity.

title: Hidden Burdens of Racial/Ethnic Concordance: An Empirical Investigation in Minnesota’s Home Visiting Programs
abstract:
In provider-routed service operations, matching providers and customers is a critical decision, particularly in high-contact, repeat-service contexts where customer retention depends on sustained relationships. Management research increasingly recognizes homophily—the tendency to connect with similar others—as a key dimension of provider-customer fit, yet its role in non-reciprocal service settings where customer participation is voluntary and free of charge remains unexplored. We examine this gap in the context of home visiting programs—public interventions providing maternal and child health support to vulnerable families. Drawing on homophily theory, we examine whether racial/ethnic concordance—matching provider and beneficiary race/ethnicity—improves retention. 

Analyzing a novel dataset of 99,318 home visits involving 5,430 beneficiaries and 88 agencies in Minnesota, we find concordance reduces beneficiary discontinuation likelihood, highlighting the role of racial homophily on beneficiary engagement. However, the effectiveness of concordance is shaped by operational conditions. Specifically, the retention benefits of concordance are attenuated in agencies with higher operational focus, suggesting that standardized, well-aligned service processes may partially substitute for relational similarity in sustaining engagement.

Beyond estimating the retention effect, we examine the operational feasibility of implementing concordant matching at scale. We show that universal racial concordance is infeasible, as it induces severe provider caseload imbalances—exceeding 300% in some agencies. Even under system-wide resource pooling across agencies, concordance rates can be increased by only 30%, with a maximum achievable rate of 60.7% due to workforce composition constraints. These findings highlight racial concordance as a powerful but capacity-constrained lever for improving retention. We conclude by outlining managerial and policy implications for expanding concordant care through workforce development and inter-agency coordination, while recognizing operational limits to race-based matching.
authors: Minjeong Kang* (University of Minnesota); Rachna Shah (University of Minnesota)
